Mr Jackson says still more pointedly: "In the interior of Africa, there is but one opinion as to the Nile of Egypt and the Nile of Tombuctoo, and that opinion is, that they are one and the same river." He adds: "The Africans express their astonishment whenever the Europeans dispute the connection of these two rivers." (p. 264.) Notwithstanding such positive assurances, it seems incontrovertibly proved by Major Rennell, that the opinion in question is totally erroneous. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERODOTUS">Herodotus</a>, indeed, mentions it, but Ptolemy, whose information was greatly superior, clearly fixes the source of the Nile among the mountains of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">Moon</a>, in a direction nearly south from Egypt. The same information was received by Mr Browne, during his residence in Darfoo, at a few hundred miles from these sources. He learned also, that all the rivers, for a great distance southwards, flowed, not east towards the Nile, but quite in the opposite direction. What is still more important,—his route intersected the only line by which there was any likelihood of the Niger joining its waters to those of the Nile. A very little way south, the country begins to rise into the great chain of the Jibbel-el-Kumri, forming a complete barrier to the passage of a river which must previously have descended to the lowest level of the plain of Soudan. But, although this point may be considered as settled, it remains still an interesting question, whether the two rivers may not communicate, by some intermediate channel, so as to form a continued navigation from Tombuctoo to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>. Mr Jackson positively asserts, that he knew a credible witness, who boasted of having actually performed this voyage. It is probable, that both the Misselad and the Kulla rise very near to the Nile, and afterwards communicate with the Niger; and it is possible, that at some point, particularly during the wet season, an union may take place. It is possible also, and perhaps more probable, that the two streams, like the Senegal and the Niger, may be considered as one, merely from approaching very near to each other. More precise testimony is necessary, in order to determine the question. In taking leave of these disputed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of African geography, we may observe, that the tract which extends southwards from the Mountains of the Moon, to the vicinity of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, forms the greatest mass of terra incognita which now exists on the surface of the globe. Reckoning from the southern frontier of Darfoo and Abyssinia, we find an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of nearly forty degrees, or two thousand four hundred miles in length, and nearly half that average breadth, which not only has not been visited by any European, but concerning which no detailed or authentic particulars have ever been received. Yet there is no reason to suppose, that it is either very thinly inhabited, or by people in the lowest stage of civilization. On the contrary, most of the limiter districts <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> with the most civilized and populous portions of this continent. On the west are the kingdoms of Loango, Congo, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANGOLA">Angola</a>; on the east are <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONOMOTAPA">Monomotapa</a>, Zanguebar, and the Somalics. Even the heights of the Jibbel-el-Kumri are found, when crossed by the Ashantee Caravan, to abound in cattle, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>, and people. The immediate vicinity of the Cape is barren and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>; but, in proportion as we advance northward, an improvement takes place. The tribes of Boshuanas recently visited, and still more those lying more remote, hold a high rank among the nations of Africa. Doubtless, there are deserts here also, and particularly a very extensive one, reaching north from the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">Orange</a> river. But there appears no probability that they should bear any proportion to those which exist on the northern side of the continent. VI. We shall conclude this article, with some miscellaneous details, regarding the present state and future prospects of this quarter of the globe. There is scarcely any question involved in greater uncertainty than the extent of its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">Population</a>. The few estimates which have been attempted are founded chiefly on random conjecture, and exhibit an extraordinary discrepancy of results. M. Golberry, who seems to have particularly attended to this subject, hesitates not to carry the amount to one hundred and sixty millions. (Voyage en Afrique.) Mr Beaufoy seems to have entertained nearly the same idea, as he estimates the interior at a hundred millions. (African Assoc. 1790.) Mr Pinkerton, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, does not conceive that it can exceed thirty, perhaps not twenty millions. M. Malte Brun names seventy millions as the utmost conceivable limit. (Precis de la Geographie. II. 560). The only principle on which any thing like an approximation can be founded seems to be this,—that the state of industry and civilization throughout cultivated Africa is so nearly the same, that the ratio of the ascertained density of any one portion may be extended to the whole. Golberry has formed a calculation, apparently pretty correct, by which he makes the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> surface of Africa to amount to one million six hundred thousand square leagues, of twenty-five to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a>, which is equal to upwards of nine millions of square geographical miles. These, at a moderate European rate, would give a population of four or five hundred millions. There are many circumstances, however, which must materially reduce the African standard. The most prominent is the immense extent of its deserts. The Sahara, with all its adjuncts, equals perhaps the whole of Europe. Its Oases, even the larger ones of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZZAN">Fezzan</a> and Darfour, though they relieve the aspect of sterility, do not materially change its general character. The former is calculated to contain only seventy-five thousand souls, the latter two hundred thousand; which will not exceed four or five to the square <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILE">mile</a>. Even the most fertile regions of Barbary and Nigritia are deeply indented with desert. We cannot, therefore, consider as exaggerated the estimate of Mr Pinkerton, that a full third of its extent is of this description. Of the remaining six millions, we think we may allow a third for those savage tracks, which, being devoid of cultivation, do not materially affect the general populousness of the continent. There will then remain four millions of square miles for cultivated Africa. Mr <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENNY">Penny</a>, a trader, who was intimately acquainted with every part of the African coast, being asked, in the Committee of Council (Report on Africa and the Slave Trade, 1788,) his ideas upon its populousness, answered as follows: He thought every one who had visited Africa and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> must have been struck with the appearance of nearly an equal population on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUINEA">Guinea</a>, and in the State of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>. Virginia contained then eight hundred thousand inhabitants, upon thirty thousand square miles, which is $26\frac{3}{4}$ to the square mile. M. Golberry is the only African traveller who has furnished any precise data upon this head. In the course of his work, he gives the population of a number of states upon the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAMBIA">Gambia</a> and Senegal, as ascertained by the French colonial administration; and we shall throw the results into the following table: | Districts | Vol. p. | Sq. Leagues | Inhabitants | |-----------|---------|-------------|------------| | Cayor | II. 102 | 2000 | 180,000 | | Sin | II. 109 | 140 | 60,000 | | Salum | II. 112 | 1500 | 300,000 | | Barra | II. 158 | 252 | 200,000 | | Bambouk | I. 432 | 1000 | 60,000 | This gives 163 to the square <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, or $26\frac{3}{4}$ to the square mile;—a result, the coincidence of which with the estimate of Mr Penny, is somewhat remarkable. Probably, therefore, we may not err very widely in fixing this as the average amount of population along the coast of Guinea, nor even in extending it to the whole of cultivated Africa. If some districts fall short of this standard, there are others of considerable extent,—as Egypt, Houssa, Tombuctoo, Whydah,—which must greatly exceed it. Four millions, then, of square miles, at the above rate, would give a population of a hundred and six millions; to which some addition must be made, though it would be difficult even to form a guess as to its amount, for the more desert and savage districts. The Commerce of Africa has always presented Commerce some peculiar features. The first and most prominent is the immense <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of land conveyance. Africa is perforated by no arms of the sea; and her rivers, though large, are imperfectly navigable, and do not flow in a convenient direction. It is by land chiefly that the merchant must find his means of exchange; and his route must lie, not on smooth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a> through smiling countries, but over an immeasurable expanse of trackless desert, where whirlwinds of sand threaten to overwhelm him at every step. To <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against these dangers, as well as to enliven the dreary <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> were naturally led to form themselves into companies, which are known under the appellation of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">Caravans</a>. The camel, an animal which nature seems to have formed expressly for travelling through the desert, is universally employed. The rate of progress is three miles an hour, and seldom more than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight hours in the day. At each of the oases, a stay of at least two days is made, for the purpose of obtaining fresh supplies of water and provisions. The following are some of the principal routes pursued by these caravans: 1. From Mourzouk, the capital of Fezzan, to Cairo; a route of about forty days. The halting places are Siwah, Augila, and Temissa. 2. From Mourzouk to Boronou; a journey of fifty days. The track is through the deserts of Bilma and Tibesti; and the principal halts are at Temissa, Domboo, and Kanem. 3. From Mourzouk to Cashna. This occupies sixty days, through Hiatts, Ganatt, and Agades. 4. From <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> to Tombuctoo, a journey of fifty-four days; but as sixty-five besides are spent in rest, the whole number of days required is one hundred and twenty-nine. The stations are Akka or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TATTA">Tatta</a>, the general rendezvous; Tegazza, and Arawan, or Arean. Another route, along the sea-coast, leads to the same point by Wedinoum, Cape Bojador, and Guatala. 5. and 6. The caravans from Sennaar and Darfour to Egypt. These do not travel so regularly as the others; and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of two or three years often elapses. The caravan with which Mr Browne travelled consisted of five hundred camels; but the number often reaches two thousand. With regard to the objects of trade, and particularly of export, these have presented a remarkable similarity, in all ages, and over every part of this continent. The first, and by far the most considerable, has always unhappily been the trade in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. Africa has in all ages been ransacked for those unfortunate beings, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a> was to be the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> or avarice to the lords of the other portions of the globe. Besides the European part of this atrocious traffic, (ere long, it is to be hoped, to be fully, and for ever relinquished,) there has long been a similar trade for the supply of Barbary and some countries of the East.* * The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and actual state of the trade in slaves, for European purposes, will be given under the head Slave Trade in this Supplement. Africa. times are drawn chiefly from the barbarous tribes inhabiting the central range of mountains. The whole number for this supply is estimated at twenty thousand. Part of these captives undergo a shameful mutilation, with the view of being placed in the seraglios of the East. In other respects, their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> is much milder than that of their West Indian brethren. They are used as domestics, are well treated, and often raised to posts of distinction. Next to the human species, the article of exchange which Africa produces most abundantly, is gold. It seems probable that its mountains contain <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of this coveted metal, more ample even than those of the new world. All the rivers which descend from the Jibbel-el-Kumri, on both sides, and throughout its whole extent, roll down sands of gold. The great repositories are Wangara, the country near the sources of the Senegal and Niger, and that immediately behind the Gold Coast. Its abundance in the districts along the Niger is said almost to surpass <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. Mr Jackson states, we suspect with exaggeration, that at Tombuctoo, it is often exchanged for its weight in salt, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>, or other valuable commodities, (p. 260.) About the beginning of the present century, the value of that exported from the gold coast, is said to have amounted to between two and three hundred thousand pounds. (Wadstrom on Colonization.) We have not been able to obtain precise information respecting the present state of this trade; for the prejudices of the mercantile system prevent gold from being classed with other commodities in the amount of exports and imports. The slave captains in their examinations before the Committee of Council, (1788) generally state, that it was too costly to be an object of trade; that it sold at L.4. an ounce, and that they did not find it their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to procure it, unless as a medium for the purchase of slaves. They admit, however, that the Dutch exported it; and the truth seems merely to be, that they found the other trade more profitable. Ivory. Next to gold, ivory has always been the great subject of African export. Like gold, it is produced almost solely in the interior, and thence brought down to the coast. Where those vast meadows lie which feed such herds of elephants, has never been ascertained; but Europe derives from Africa its whole supply of this valuable article. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">Gum</a>. Gum, particularly Gum Senegal, forms an important branch of trade. The southern parts of the desert of Sahara contain vast forests of that species of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACACIA">acacia</a>, from which this substance exudes. In the month of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, a dry and piercing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> bursts the bark, and the juice flows out. The neighbouring Moorish tribes then leave their habitations, and employ themselves for six weeks in collecting it; after which they repair to the banks of the Senegal, to exchange it for European commodities. The price is first fixed by a meeting of the merchants with their kings and chiefs. This point being settled, in a few days the Moors appear in vast bands, with their wives, children, and cattle; and for some days, a tumultuous market is held. M. Golberry calculates, that two millions of pounds of gum may be drawn from this part of Africa. (Travels, chap. vi.) Among the valuable productions of this country, we may also mention <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HIDES">hides</a> and skins, particularly goatskins dyed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>. These are brought by the caravans from central Africa to <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a>, whence they are exported to Europe, chiefly from the port of Mogador. Africa exports likewise ornamental and dye woods, particularly red or cam wood, to a very considerable extent. Raw hides and bees wax have, within the last few years, become considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. There are doubtless many other <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> and local objects; but those now enumerated may be considered as forming the basis of African export. It is remarkable that, with the exception of a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, the whole consists, not merely of the unmanufactured, but of the spontaneous produce of the land. So small is the progress yet made by cultivation throughout this great continent. The imports are limited, by the limited wants of the climate and state of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> most in demand are checked cottons, light coarse cloths, red woollen caps, a few linens and silks, and a large proportion of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIA">India</a> piece-goods. Spirits, chiefly rum, are too much in demand; guns and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, hardware, chiefly in the form of knives, sabres, blades; <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, which is manufactured into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAR">ear</a>-rings; coral, beads, looking-glasses, and other articles of ornament. The scarcity of salt causes a certain import from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, even of that bulky article. 1,156,985| 1,655,042| 1,022,745| 820,194| 976,872| 693,911| On adverting to the future prospects of Africa, it is proper to say something, in the first place, as to the means of its more perfect exploration. It seems, then, to be now universally admitted, that no reliance can be placed on the common <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of solitary enterprise, or where the traveller has only one or two attendants. Nor is the device of assuming the character of a Mahometan likely to be repeated. Mahometanism is not a <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> creed; it is a system, which regulates the whole train of thoughts and habits, and which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOULDS">moulds</a> from infancy even the outward aspect and deportment. It is vain to expect, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of Arabic at an European seminary, or even a few months residence in the East, could mould all the habits of an European into a shape, which would enable him to deceive the watchful eyes of Musulmen. It appears also, that, while the character of a professed Christian is sufficiently detested, that of one who assumes a false semblance of Mahometanism is viewed with a much higher degree of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-REPROBATION">reprobation</a>. To the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, therefore, which Hornemann assumed, it is probable that this unfortunate traveller was partly indebted for his melancholy fate. The only <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a>, then, it would appear, of penetrating into Africa, with any prospect of success, is to carry an armed force, which shall not be so large as to excite alarm, and yet sufficient to guard against desultory or sudden attack. Such an expedition would the less tend to excite jealousy, that Africa is habitually traversed by parties of this description for commercial purposes. Yet it is remarkable, that the two attempts which have been made upon this plan have terminated still more fatally than those in which no such precautions had been taken,—we allude to the last expedition of Park, and that sent by Lord Caledon from the Cape of Good Hope. These failures, however, we regret to say, seem to have been the result of such obvious imprudence, as not to authorize any inference against the general superiority of this plan. Park, by unluckily <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> his party to be destroyed by the rainy season, reduced himself to the same unprotected state with former travellers. The expedition from the Cape was too small; and yet, till they gave way to supine security, and sacrificed all the advantages of their strength by dividing it, no hostile attempt appears to have been made. The editor of Park's last journal recommends an expedition on a large scale, to be composed chiefly of African soldiers enlisted at Sierra Leone; but we cannot help feeling some doubts as to the safety of an expedition, in which the majority should be Africans. And as this writer suggests the propriety of employing a traveller from the East, we would add, that his attendants should rather be Scapoys than Africans. The plan upon which the main reliance for the civilization of this region seems at present to be placed is, that of an extensive system of colonization. It is observed by Mr Macaulay, Ex-secretary of the African <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">Institution</a>, that it is "necessary to the rapid growth of improvement, that men should be brought together in considerable bodies; that they should be protected by just laws; and that they should enjoy the means of instruction." This, he conceives, can only be effected in Africa by means of a colony, of some extent, composed of natives. The difficulty of collecting a large native population is admitted, indeed, to be very great. The Africans, from many causes, and particularly from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, will not voluntarily <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to such a colony. A plan had, therefore, been suggested, in reference to the co- --- *These tables exhibit a curious view of the effects of the abolition. Almost all the articles of import have remarkably increased, and their general amount has more than doubled. The exports have necessarily suffered a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REDUCTION">reduction</a>, which, however, has taken place almost wholly in the articles of guns, spirits, and (we know not exactly why,) of India piece-goods; while British manufactures maintain nearly their former amount.* AFRICAN ASSOCIATION. See Association, African, in the Encyclopedia. AFRICAN <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">COMPANY</a>. The reader will find, under the head Company, in the body of the Work, an account of the formation of this establishment, and the footing on which it at present stands. Though instituted for commercial purposes, it is now prohibited from trading in its corporate capacity; and its functions are limited to maintaining the forts on the Gold Coast; a sum for that purpose being annually allowed by <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a>. In the Report of the Commissioners appointed to inquire into the state of the African Settlements, in 1812, the following is stated to be the annual expense of each of these forts: | Fort | Expense (£) | |---------------|-------------| | Appolonia | 879 | | Dixcove | 926 | | Succondee | 429 | | Commenda | 842 | | Cape Coast Castle | 4,768 | | Annamaboe | 1,885 | | Tantumquery | 771 | | Winnebah | 776 | | Accra | 1,328 | | Whydah | 587 | Total: £13,195 The whole annual expenses of the Company in Africa, for forts, salaries of officers, &c. is stated to be £25,327, 18. 5½d. It further appears from this Report, that the trade of the coast is chiefly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Governors of the forts, to each of whom it affords a perquisite of from £800 to £1,000 a year. Their local knowledge and influence give them an advantage, with which ships coming from a distance cannot compete. Cape Coast forms the only exception, as there are several European agents residing there. The number of forts appeared to the Committee to be much greater than is necessary for maintaining the British influence upon this coast; and in consequence, Winnebah and Whydah were abandoned, which has so far reduced the annual expense. The Company were recently called upon to explain the reason of their sending out goods, which did not appear necessary for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of their settlements. To this they answered, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> 23 Geo. II. ch. 31, by which they were constituted, expressly authorizes them to make their African payments in goods; that the remittance of the salaries of their servants in any other form would be attended with great inconvenience, both to the Company and to individuals; and that the profit made upon these goods enables the Company, with an annual <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> of £23,000, to support an expenditure in Africa of £25,000, and to defray the expenses of management at home. The Company's charges at home, consist of £100 to each of the nine members of the committee; and £300 to the secretary; in all £1,200. The number of persons in their employ, at Christmas 1813, consisted of 47 Governors and subordinate officers; 450 soldiers and menials; and they had thirty seven Negro chiefs in their pay. (n.) AFRICAN INSTITUTION. This Institution was formed in 1807, for purposes which, to use the words of a celebrated Literary Journal, "certainly render it one of the most interesting, and most creditable to the feelings and character of our country, that ever found support within its bounds." (Edinb. Review, Vol. XV. p. 485.) Its general objects, and the views which influenced its formation, are clearly stated in the following resolutions adopted, at the constituent meeting, held on the 14th of April 1807. "1. That this meeting is deeply impressed with a sense of the enormous <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WRONGS">wrongs</a> which the natives of African Institutions in promoting any of the purposes of the institution." (First Report, p. 4.) The management of the affairs of this institution is vested in a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, twenty vice-presidents, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a>, and a board of thirty-six directors. These officers are chosen annually from among that class of the subscribers who are called governors of the institution. Those who subscribe sixty guineas at one time become <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> governors; but thirty guineas subscribed at one time, make the subscriber a governor for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; or three guineas annually, a governor during the continuance of this annual subscription. Every subscriber of one guinea becomes an ordinary member, and continues so during the continuance of his subscription. It is much to be regretted, that the funds of this noble institution are far too limited to enable it to pursue with vigour those great objects which it was intended to promote. Its annual income does not exceed £400; and, including donations, its whole receipts, of every kind, from its first formation to the commencement of the present year (1815), have amounted to only £9350. With such scanty means, it is impossible to do much in a direct way towards the advancement of civilization. A single fact will suffice to show this. To a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> teacher lately sent to Sierra Leone, the society allows a salary of £300 a-year, and this sum, moderate as it is, exhausts three-fourths of its annual income. But though the Institution has not hitherto been enabled to commence any extended plans of civilization in Africa, it has happily been able to aid materially in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> the way for such plans, by exerting its influence to effect a thorough abolition of the slave trade. This is the first great and indispensable step towards the improvement of Africa; and the vigilant attention of the society to this primary object has been of the greatest importance, both by enforcing a rigorous execution of the abolition laws enacted in this country, and by animating and directing the public call upon other nations to follow our example. The proceedings of the society are fully detailed in its annual Reports, which are regularly published. These Reports are written with great ability, and contain much valuable and interesting information in regard to Africa, and the means of civilizing it. It may be proper to add, that the conduct of the directors has been severely attacked, and their Reports criticised, in a pamphlet lately published by Dr Thorpe, who, for sometime, held the office of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">Chief</a> Judge in the colony of Sierra Leone. The directors have replied to his accusations with great temper, and, in so far as we can judge, with complete success, in a Special Report, read at a general meeting in April last (1815), and since published.

AGNESI

Pages 335-336

an Italian lady, who may be justly pronounced one of the greatest wonders and ornaments of her <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILAN">Milan</a> on the 16th of May 1718. Our materials for an account of this celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> are by no means so complete, nor in some interesting particulars so distinct, as we could have wished. Not having been able to procure her Eloge by Frisi; we have been obliged to content ourselves with some shorter notices; the most detailed of which is that contained in Mazzucchelli's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of the Writers of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> published during the earlier, but more brilliant <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. The accounts which this writer and some others have given of the intellectual capacities and endowments which she displayed in early youth, call to mind the wonders which have been related of Picus of Mirandula, and the Admirable Crichton. Nor does there seem any reason to doubt their authenticity. At <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, she not only spoke the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> with precision, but even composed and delivered an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORATION">oration</a> in that language, intended to prove that the cultivation of letters is not incompatible with the female character. This singular piece was published at Milan the same year in which it was spoken, with the following <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>: Oratio qua ostenditur artium liberium studia a feminino sexu nequitiam abhorrere, habita a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> de Agnesii rhetoricae operam dante anno octatis sue nono nondum exacto, die 18 Augusti 1727. At eleven years of age, she spoke Greek with all the fluency of her native tongue. When yet very young, she had also acquired some of the languages of the East; and, in a word, her acquisitions as a linguist were such, as to procure for her the appellation of a Walking Polyglott. But her aptitude for acquiring languages, however <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, was by no means the only, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the most striking feature of her intellectual character. We have seen how early she essayed the discussion of a general question affecting the mental capacities of her sex, and the vigour and acuteness displayed in this aspiring <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">essay</a> were, ere <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a>, exerted with ardour and success in scientific inquiries. Having gone through the elementary branches of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>, she proceeded with alacrity to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY"><a class="xref" hr</a>ef="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and she seems also to have carried her researches into the obscurer regions of metaphysical speculation. About the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when she reached her fifteenth year, her father formed a select <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> of the learned of Milan, and at these meetings, which were held in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, at stated times, for several years, Agnesi maintained a succession of Theorems on various <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of speculation and philosophy. The ability which she displayed on these occasions seems to have been altogether surprising; and the effect was not the less, that her person was agreeable, and her whole deportment gentle and prepossessing. We are indebted to the learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> De Brosse for the following account of one of these conferences, at which he assisted during his travels in Italy, through the introduction of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Belloni. "I had conceived," says he, "when I went to this conversation, that it was only to talk with this young lady in the usual way, though on learned subjects; but to my surprise, Belloni addressed her in a fine Latin <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARANGUE">harangue</a>, with all the formality of an academic oration. She replied in the same language, with prompt- ness and ability; and they proceeded, still in Latin, to discuss the origin of fountains, and the causes of the ebbs and flows observed in some of them. She spoke like an angel on this subject, and I never heard it treated so much to my satisfaction. We then discoursed with her concerning the manner in which the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> receives impressions from outward objects, and their conveyance to the general sensorium, the brain; and afterwards upon the propagation of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and the prismatic colours. The conversation afterwards became general, every one speaking to her in the language of his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and she answering in the same." (Lettres sur l'Italie, Tom. I. p. 243.) But Agnesi seems to have taken but little delight in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> which she acquired as a philosophical disputant. Her temper was retired and devout, and she appears to have acted this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> more to gratify her father than herself. About her twentieth year, she accordingly withdrew from these assemblies, and for a long period devoted the greater part of her time to mathematical studies. The Theses which she had maintained with so much applause were published in a quarto volume, under the following title: Propositiones Philosophice quas crebris disputationibus domi habitis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CORAM">coram</a> clarissimis viris explicabit extempore et <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> objectis vindicabat Maria Gaetana de Agnesii Mediolanensis, Med. 1738. The first fruit of her mathematical studies was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMENTARY">Commentary</a> on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a> of the Marquis de l'<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOSPITAL">Hospital</a>; but this piece she would never consent to publish, though Mazzucchelli says that it was greatly praised by many who had perused the manuscript. In the course of a few years, however, she gave to the world a mathematical work, which must ever secure her a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> among the most distinguished cultivators of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSTRACT">abstract</a> science. This work, entitled Instituzioni Analitiche <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> uso della Gioventù Italiana, was published at Milan in 1748, in two volumes quarto. The first volume treats of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of finite quantities; the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, of the analysis of infinitesimals. These two volumes contain a full and satisfactory view of this branch of mathematical science in the state at which it had then arrived; and though improvements have since that time been introduced, the treatise of Agnesi, according to a very competent authority, may still be regarded as perhaps the best introduction that is to be found to the works of Euler, and the other mathematicians of the Continent. (Edinb. Review, Vol. III. p. 408.)—An English translation of this work was long ago executed by the late Professor Golson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, but the manuscript lay buried in obscurity for many years, and was only published in 1801, through the care and at the expense of Baron Maseres. Besides other literary honours which followed the publication of the Analytical Institutions, Agnesi was, in 1750, appointed Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. The appointment of a young female, of thirty-two years of age, to such a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, must appear to many --- *This Eloge has been translated into French by Boulard, and published both separately, and at the end of a work entitled, Bienfaits de la <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a> Chrétienne, 2 vols. Svo, 1807. See Biographie Universelle, Tom. I.*

AGUESSEAU

Pages 429-460

a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">Chancellor</a> of France, illustrious for his virtues, learning, and talents, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMOGES">Limoges</a> on the 27th of November 1668. His father, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> Intendant of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>, and afterwards a Counsellor of State; was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> worth and abilities. He seems to have taken the sole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his son's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>; and having destined him for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>, he took uncommon pains to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> him in every branch of knowledge which could contribute to his success in that profession. His care was rewarded with the happiest success. Young D'Aguesseau gave early indications of uncommon abilities; and such was his thirst for knowledge, and his habits of application, that he soon acquired the reputation of an almost universal scholar. He had a particular relish for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which he used to say, "was the only <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> of his youth;" but this passion was so far from withdrawing him from severer studies, that it was allied in his mind with a nearly equal <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>. He studied <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> with the zeal of an antiquary, and the spirit of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>; and, in order to form his taste as a pleader, he employed a whole year in repeated perusals of the most esteemed productions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> eloquence. After this thorough course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, he became an advocate in 1690; and, by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of his father, who now resided in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, he was soon furnished with opportunities of distinguishing himself, and of rising to the highest honours of the profession. When little more than twenty-one years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was appointed one of the three <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">Advocates</a>-general—an office which imposed the duty of assisting in those causes where the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the public were concerned. The king, (<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV.) in appointing him, yet untried, to this D'Aguesseau situation, acted solely upon the recommendation of the elder D'Aguesseau, "who was incapable," said Louis, "of deceiving him, even to advance his own son." D'Aguesseau's first appearances as an advocate-general were such as amply to fulfil the expectations of his father, and to warrant the appointment which he had obtained from the king. Denis Talon, an old lawyer, who had <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> officiated, with great reputation, in the same capacity, was heard to say, "that he should have been glad to have finished his <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CAREER">career</a> as that young man had begun." D'Aguesseau held this office for ten years; during which <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he greatly distinguished himself, both for learning in his profession, and for a superior style of forensic eloquence. He was, indeed, one of the first reformers of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of the French bar, which had not yet taken much polish from the national improvements in taste and literature. His diction, both in his pleadings and in his juridical compositions, was that of a mind expanded by a liberal course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>, and refined by a familiar acquaintance with classical models. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> which he chiefly frequented was also well adapted to improve his taste; for the chosen companions of his leisure hours were Racine and Boileau; the latter of whom has frequently mentioned him with praise in his writings. It was D'Aguesseau's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that no one could rise to distinguished eminence as an orator, who did not labour to enlarge and polish his mind by the study of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and by exercises of literature; and he accordingly employed several of those stated discourses, which the usages of France required from the advocates-general at the opening of the sessions, to impress this doctrine upon the minds of the younger members of the bar. Such, in particular, was the object of his discourse, pronounced in 1695, *Sur l'Union de la Philosophie et de l'Eloquence*. The same subject is treated at greater length, and in a more systematic and preceptive manner, in a treatise, written at a later period, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of *Instructions sur l'Etude et les Exercices qui peuvent preparer aux Fonctions d'Avocat du Roi*. These pieces (*Œuvres*, Tom. I.) are written in a clear, manly, and harmonious style, and are well worthy the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the general scholar, for their critical strictures on those authors whom he recommends to the students of law. In the year 1700 he was appointed *Procureur-general*—an office of higher <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and imposing more various and extensive duties, than that of advocate-general. He filled this office for seventeen years with the most splendid reputation; adding, by his lenity in criminal <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol3.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, and by his care of the public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a>, the praise of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a> and benevolence to his other claims to the admiration of his countrymen. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> philosopher of the present <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> probably, however, be inclined to question the justness of the encomiums bestowed upon his exertions during the severe scarcity of 1709; on which occasion, he appears to have instituted the most rigorous proceedings against those who were held up as enemies of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and of mankind, under the names of forestallers and monopolists. But, in alluding to this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of his conduct, it may be proper to mention, that his opposition, at an after period, to the delusive projects of the famous John Law, and his elaborate treatise upon the subject of *<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">Money</a>*, (*Œuvres*, Tom. X.) afford undeniable proofs of the soundness of his views, in regard to some of the most important principles of political economy. It had been early predicted of D'Aguiseau, that he would one day fill the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Chancellor; and this prediction was at length realized in 1717, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Voisin, who then held the seals. Though he was yet little more than forty-eight years of age, his nomination to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> dignity gave general satisfaction; and was, indeed, intended as a popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORLEANS">Orleans</a>, who had lately assumed the regency. His <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> Valjouan, a man of abilities, but slothful and a humorist, was the only person who spoke with indifference on the occasion. "Rather you than I, brother," was his only remark when the new Chancellor hastened to him to announce his appointment. In fact, D'Aguiseau was soon made to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> the storms attendant upon this lofty station; for he had not been installed above a year, when he was deprived of the seals, and exiled to his estate. His steady opposition to the extravagant projects of Law, with which the regent and his ministers were wholly intoxicated, was the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> cause of this first reverse of his fortune. In 1720, when the ruinous consequences of these schemes had filled the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> with distress and alarm, the chancellor was recalled from banishment; and he contributed not a little, by the firmness and sagacity of his counsels, to calm the public murmurs, and repair the mischief which had been committed. Law himself had acted as the messenger of his recall; and it is said, that D'Aguiseau's consent to re-accept the seals from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of this adventurer, was much blamed by the literary corps, with which he had hitherto stood in high favour, as well as by the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. But his reputation appears to have sustained a much severer shock, when he endeavoured to prevail with the latter body, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECLARATION">declaration</a> of the late king in favour of the famous bull *Unigenitus*—a measure which they held in great abhorrence, and which he had himself firmly opposed during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>. The regent's favourite Dubois, then Archbishop of Cambrai, had moved his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> to insist upon this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of registration, in the hope that he might thereby obtain for himself a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a>'s hat; and it seems to have been thought, that the Chancellor had yielded his better opinion in compliance with the wishes of this worthless minion. Be this as it may, it is certain that he opposed the favourite with firmness, when he attempted, after being made prime minister, to take precedence in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>; and he was in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, in 1722, sent a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> time into exile. He now passed five years on his estate at Fresnes; and he always spoke with delight of this tranquil period, when he was left free from the cares of professional duty, and the distractions of public life, to cultivate his mind. The Scriptures, which he read and compared in various languages, and the laws of his own and other countries, formed the subjects of his more serious studies; the rest of his time was devoted to philosophy and literature, and the improvement of his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARK">park</a>, where he was sometimes to be seen employed with a spade. From these noble and congenial occupations he was again recalled, by the advice of Cardinal Fleury, in 1727; but the seals were not restored to him till ten years thereafter. During the intervening period, he had endeavoured to mediate in the new disputes which had arisen between the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> and the parliament; but his interference seems to have given satisfaction to neither party; the one reproaching him with desertion from their cause, and the other with too great a leaning towards it. When the seals were at last restored to him, he completely withdrew from all affairs of state, and devoted himself entirely to his duties as Chancellor, and to the introduction of those reforms which had long occupied his inquiries and meditations. Besides some important enactments regarding Testaments, Successions, and Donations, he introduced various regulations for improving the forms of procedure,—for ascertaining the limits of Jurisdictions,—and for effecting a greater uniformity in the execution of the laws throughout the several provinces. These reforms constitute a sort of epoch in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a> of France, and have associated his name with those illustrious benefactors of her Civil Code,—L'Hopital and Lamoignon. The Duke de Saint-Simon however, alleges, that the Chancellor's reforms did not go so far as they would have gone, had he had less affection for his own order. He once, says this writer, confessed to a nobleman who spoke to him upon the propriety of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off certain lucrative abuses, that he could not bring his mind to a step which would so grievously diminish the profits of the law. In 1750, when upwards of eighty-two years of age, he besought the king to accept his resignation; and he was accordingly permitted to retire, the king continuing to him the honours of his office as a special mark of his approbation. He died in the following year; and was interred, according to his own request, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a>-place of the village of Auteuil, where the remains of his wife, who died there in 1735, had been deposited. The name of this lady, whom he married in 1694, and by whom he had several children, was <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Le Fevre d'Ormesson. This great man has not, in all respects, been equally praised by those, who have, in their writings, transmitted his character to posterity. Saint-Simon and others reproach him with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of tardiness and indecision in his judgments, which sometimes greatly obstructed the course of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. His own answer to this charge has been recorded by Duclos, and is worthy of notice: "When I recollect," said he, "that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> of a Chancellor is a law, I think myself warranted in taking a long time for consideration." Saint-Simon and D'Argenson also impute to him some defects as a statesman; but his elevation of mind and extensive knowledge, his piety, probity, and disinterestedness, have been universally admitted and extolled. In his magisterial capacity, he was <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and dignified, without any approach to haughtiness; in private society, his manners were mild, equal, and even playful. He was particularly remarkable for the tenaciousness of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>, and for the facility with which he could <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> his attention to the most diversified exercises of intellect or imagination. At eighty years of age, he has been heard to repeat whole poems, which he had never perused since the days of his early youth; and when fatigued with professional duties, he could turn with equal alacrity to Euclid or to Racine. In summing up his character, all must agree with La Harpe, that he was "a man who did <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to France, to the magistracy, and to letters, by his virtues, his talents, his profound and various learning, and his enlightened views in the science of jurisprudence." (Cours de Litterature, Tom. XIV. c. 1.) His published writings form a collection of thirteen volumes quarto; of which the first volume was published at Paris in 1759, and the last in 1789. The far greater part of these volumes relate to matters connected with his professional character and studies; but they also contain a variety of pieces upon miscellaneous subjects. We have already mentioned his discourses on the studies befitting the students of law, and his treatise on Money; and besides these, and some theological pieces, there is a Life of his Father, interesting from the view which it affords of his own early education under that excellent person; together with "Metaphysical Meditations," written in vindication of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that, independently of all <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>, and all positive law, there is that in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> mind which renders man a law to himself. See Histoire des Hommes Illustres de Regnes de Louis XIV. et de Louis XV. par le Duc de Saint-Simon. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> Secreces, par Duclos. Les Loisirs d'un Ministre d'Etat, par D'Argenson. Eloge de D'Aguiseau, par Thomas. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">AIR</a>. We had intended to exhibit, in a collected view, the various properties, physical and chemical, of this important <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> fluid; and also to have given the results of some original researches on its relations to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>; but as our experimental inquiries, undertaken with this view, are not yet completed, we shall refer the whole to a more comprehensive article. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">Atmosphere</a>.

ALBANIA

Pages 460-463

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of considerable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, which, though in fact nearly independent, forms nominally one of the provinces of the Turkish empire. It extends from the thirty-ninth to the forty-third <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> latitude, for the space of about 250 miles, along the Mediterranean and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GULF">Gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>. The extent inland nowhere exceeds one hundred miles; and is, in the southern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a>, not more than thirty. The chain of Pindus, called now the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Sagori, of Metzovo, and of Suli, separate it, by an ill defined line, from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACEDONIA">Macedonia</a> and Thessaly. The Turks divided it into Pashalics; of which the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> are those of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SCUTARI">Scutari</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-OCHRIDA">Ochrida</a>, Vallenia, and Butrinto; but these distinctions, in its present state of independence, are in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> obliterated. The divisions chiefly recognized are those formed by the varieties of the native tribes. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAJOR">Major</a> Leake, who is allowed to be the best informed traveller on this head, divides them into the Ngeze, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Ghegides, whose principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> are Dulcigno, Scutari, and Durazzo; the Toske, or Toskides, who occupy Berat and Elbasan; the Liapce, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and predatory <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, who inhabit the mountains between the Toske and Delvino; and the Tsami, who inhabit the most southerly district, and whose principal towns are Suli and Paramithia. There are, besides, a great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of smaller divisions, too tedious to enumerate. (Leake's Researches in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a>.) Albania nearly coincides with the country known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, under the name of Epirus. This country was then, as now, distinguished by the rude valour of its inhabitants. Its remote situation, and the want of union among its tribes, generally prevented it from acting any conspicuous part in Grecian politics. The only remarkable exception occurs in the reign of Pyrrhus II., who was justly ranked with the greatest captains of antiquity. After his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, the country was again split into a number of petty states, which were unable to resist the united strength of Macedon; and to that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, Epirus <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> subject, till both were alike subdued by the Roman arms. It was during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Greek empire, that the name of Albania was first given to this district. During the decline of the empire, the Albanians gradually rose to distinction, and at last to independence. Their valour enabled them to maintain their ground against the Bulgarians, who had occupied all the neighbouring districts of Greece. Nor were they less successful against the Turks, a more formidable enemy. Under the command of the celebrated George Castriot, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCANDERBEG">Scanderbeg</a>, they baffled all the efforts of Mahomet II., the conqueror of Constantinople. That powerful monarch entered Albania only to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a> a succession of defeats, and was at length compelled to acknowledge its independence by a formal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a>. On the death of Scanderbeg, the Turks redoubled their efforts against Albania, which was at length reduced to a state of nominal subjection. The siege of Scutari, in 1478, formed the termination of this memorable struggle. The subjection, however, was always imperfect; revolts were frequent, and the inhabitants of the mountainous districts still preserved their independence. It was by the motives of pay and plunder, rather than by compulsion, that these hardy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> were allured into the Turkish ranks. In proportion as the Ottoman empire declined in vigour, its hold of Albania became less and less firm; and the vigorous and enterprising genius of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a> Pasha, has now again converted this dependency into what may almost be called a separate kingdom. Ali was born at Tepellene, a small town in the interior of Albania. His father held the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of a Pasha of two tails, but was not possessed of any extensive power; and he died when Ali was only fifteen. In a district so turbulent, and filled with warlike and hostile leaders, the young <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> was necessarily placed in a very critical situation. He is himself accustomed to boast, that he began his fortune with sixty paras and a musket; and an Albanian who attended a late traveller (Mr Hobhouse) declared, that he remembered to have seen Ali with his jacket out at elbows. Ali was ere <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> driven from Tepellene, his native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and was abandoned by almost every follower. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> was next formed for his destruction, by the inhabitants of Gardiki, a neighbouring town; and for this purpose, they surrounded, in the night time, a village where he had taken refuge. Ali escaped through a garden, but his mother and sister fell into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Gardikiotes, and were treated with every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of indignity; <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-WRONGS">wrongs</a> for which he afterwards took a dreadful vengeance. His <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADDRESS">address</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a> enabled him gradually to repair his fortunes. He insinuated himself into the favour of Coul Pasha, then the principal chief of Albania, whose <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> he at length married. Having thus been enabled to collect some followers, he succeeded in surprising his present <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, Joannina, and in prevailing upon the Porte to recognize him as Pacha of that important district. From this time, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> among the Albanian chiefs; employing sometimes force, sometimes <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and sometimes treachery, to increase his authority, and add to the extent of his dominions. The most formidable adversaries with whom Ali had to contend, were the Suliotes, a people placed in the southern extremity of Albania. They inhabit an almost inaccessible range of mountains, beneath whose gloomy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a> winds a river, which Dr <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> conjectures, on very plausible grounds, to be the Acheron of the ancients. (Travels in the Ionian Isles and Albania.) The strength of their native bulwarks, their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, and contempt of death, made them the terror of Albania, which they frequently invaded; while no foreign power had ever ventured to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> the tremendous barriers by which they were guarded. Ali at length succeeded, partly by force, and partly by bribery, in gaining the passes which led into their country; and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, after a furious resistance, was reduced to subjection, and partly extirpated. In 1811 and 1812, Ali attacked and defeated the Pashas of Berat and Delvino; by which means he gained possession of some of the finest parts of Albania, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of between 200,000 and 300,000 souls. Tepellene, his native place, now fell into his power; and now also it was, that he obtained the means of inflicting signal vengeance on Gardiki. With his accustomed duplicity, he pretended a complete oblivion of all grounds of resentment, until he had surrounded and enclosed the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> with his troops; when upwards of 700 of those of the inhabitants who were supposed to have been most deeply involved in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> guilt, were dragged into a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> khan near the city, and bound together with cords. On a signal given by Ali, the Albanian soldiery, who were stationed on the walls of the khan, began a discharge of musketry, which continued until the destruction of the whole 700 was completed. It seems impossible to define with perfect precision, either the extent of Ali's dominions, or the degree of authority which he possesses. Even within Albania, the Pachalic of Scutari remains still independent. The tract over which he bears sway, is bounded on the north by an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> line, extending from Durazzo to the Gulf of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SALONICA">Salonica</a>. It comprehends the mountainous district of Macedonia, nearly the whole of Thessaly, and great part of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIVADIA">Livadia</a>. On the eastern side, he is kept in check by Ismael Bey, who possesses an authority nearly as independent over the plains of Macedonia. In Albania, his power is almost <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a>; and while little regard is paid to the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIRMAN">firman</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> with the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SIGNATURE">signature</a> of Ali commands implicit obedience. The Albanians are enthusiastically attached to him; they view him as a native sovereign; they admire the energy of his character, and when they hear of any other chief, commonly remark, that "he has not a head like Ali." In the relations between Ali and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of Constantinople, mutual fear has hitherto preserved an outward good understanding. The progress of this enterprising chief has been long viewed with jealousy and alarm; but the Porte was never in a condition to hazard driving him into open rebellion. It has been found prudent, therefore, to invest him, by its firman, with the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of those provinces which the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> had already placed in his possession. Ali, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, pays an outward deference to the Porte; and remits to it some portion of the revenue which he collects. He has also uniformly supported that power with nearly his whole force, against the foreign enemies with which it has had to contend. He even marched against Paswan Oglou, and was present at the siege of Widdin; and his son Mouctar Pasha, distinguished himself greatly in the late war against the Russians. In all other respects, whether as to the internal government of Albania, or its foreign relations, he acts completely as an independent monarch. The Porte has omitted no means of inducing him to repair to Constantinople, and has even proffered to him the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> Vizier; but Ali has uniformly resisted every such invitation, well knowing that his arrival at that capital would be the immediate signal for striking off his head. Buonaparte is also believed to have courted his favour, and to have offered him the dignity of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">King</a> of Albania; but the Pasha always viewed the ambitious designs of that conqueror with alarm, and attached himself to England; with the politics and interests of which country, it appears from his conversations with Dr Holland, he was tolerably well acquainted. The natives estimate Ali's <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> force so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as fifty, sixty, or even 100,000 men. This could only apply to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a general levy en masse, in the event of invasion. It does not appear that Ali has ever brought into the field a greater disposable force than 15,000. His standing <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> is supposed to be about 10,000, of whom 4,000 or 5,000 are stationed round his capital Joannina. The amount of his revenues is still more uncertain. They arise from the following sources: 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> tax, amounting generally to about 10 per cent of the produce. 2. A tax on cities and towns, levied in the form of requisition. 3. The customs, which he has raised to six per cent. 4. The inheritance of all who die without <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> heirs. There are several <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">minor</a> sources; and besides his public revenue, Ali is supposed to possess private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to the amount of 4,000,000 piastres, or L. 200,000 per annum. It seems impossible to conjecture, either what may be the amount of his entire revenue, or what proportion he remits to Constantinople; but it is generally believed, that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> which he has accumulated is very considerable. Ali is now (1815) sixty or sixty-one years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> is corpulent and unwieldy, his neck short, his stature about five feet <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> inches. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of his countenance is striking and majestic; and his features give no indications of those terrible qualities by which he is characterized. His abilities are certainly of no <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> order. He displays that union of deep thought and contrivance, with prompt and decisive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, which indicates a mind equally formed for politics and for war. He is remarkable for his address, both in gaining friends, and in lulling asleep the suspicions of his bitterest enemies. But, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his abilities are of a superior order, his dispositions are of a kind which render him an object of fear and detestation. His cruelty rather resembles that of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a>, than of even the least civilized European. Impaling, and roasting alive, are among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> punishments reserved for those who have unhappily offended him. The fierceness of his cruelty is only exceeded by the depth of his dissimulation. It is impossible for the most skilful observer to conjecture, from his outward deportment, the real sentiments with which he regards any individual. The only observable <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, consists in a peculiar kindness of manner, towards those unfortunates, whose cruel doom he has silently and unrelentingly sealed. Ali's ordinary residence is near Joannina, in an immense <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which combines the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> and a fortress. The outer courts are irregularly crowded with Albanian soldiers, and with persons of all descriptions, who attend upon, or have petitions to present to him. Each petitioner, in approaching, kneels and kisses his garment. He exercises in person the whole judicial authority; and his decisions, though necessarily given too promptly, are however said to be guided by an apparent wish of arriving at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and of doing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>. It may be supposed that this employment, joined to a minute <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to every other part of his administration, must fully occupy his time. Accordingly, he rises at six in the morning, and with the exception of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> at dinner, and an hour at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUPPER">supper</a>, spends the whole <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> in business. His habits at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> are extremely temperate, though he is not so strict a Musulman as to decline the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of wine. His haram contains three hundred females of various descriptions. It forms an edifice entirely distinct from the rest of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERAGLIO">seraglio</a>, and is said to be furnished in a style of the most gorgeous magnificence; but no European has hitherto found admission into it. Although the government of Ali is completely <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESPOTICAL">despotical</a>, yet, viewed comparatively, it appears to be better for Albania, than the terrible anarchy to which it was formerly exposed. He has freed that country from a race of petty tyrants, and from perpetual scenes of internal warfare. His vigorous administration has nearly extirpated those numerous predatory hordes, who found shelter in the mountainous districts, and spread terror and desolation over the plains. The inhabitants of Albania are estimated at twelve hundred thousand; those of Ali's whole dominions at two millions. Albania contains a considerable proportion of Turks and Greeks; but the basis of the population, and that in which Ali places his chief confidence, consists of its original race. This remarkable people differ completely from every other included within the limits of the Turkish empire. Their conversion to Mahometan tenets has been very imperfect, and chiefly induced by <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> motives. In every family the males usually go to the mosque, the females to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>; and some members of a family are seen in the most <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMICABLE">amicable</a> manner eating from the same table, and even from the same plate, meats forbidden to the others. With the Turks, accordingly, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INFIDEL">infidel</a> and Albanian are terms nearly <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a>. Ali himself, does not appear to make <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> a ground of any the slightest distinction between the different classes of his subjects.
