The native Albanian is of a middle stature; his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> is oval, with high cheek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; his neck long, his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHEST">chest</a> full and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is erect and majestic, to a degree which never fails to surprise the traveller. He holds in utter contempt that dissimulation which is characteristic of the Greek, and piques himself upon giving utterance to every sentiment without the smallest reserve. Equally remote from the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a> and sluggish deportment of the Turk, he is gay, lively, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a>. Averse, however, to regular industry, his whole delight is in arms and plunder. He goes constantly armed; and there are few Albanians who, in the prime of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, have not belonged to some of the numerous bands of robbers, who infest the mountains of their native country, of Thessaly, and of Macedonia. This profession carries with it no disgrace; it is common for the Albanian to mention circumstances which occurred, "when he was a robber." In proportion as the trade of robbing becomes overstocked, part of those engaged in it seek employment in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>, and of the different Pashas throughout the Turkish empire; by all of whom the Albanians are regarded as the most valuable of their troops. An Albanian military force, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of Dr Holland, cannot so properly be called an army, as a tumultuous assemblage of armed men. There is no regular distribution into corps; nor is much regard paid to the authority of any officer, with the single exception of the Pasha himself. Yet, such is their activity and intrepidity, that they have sometimes proved formidable to the best disciplined European armies. Whatever was done in the last Turkish <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAMPAIGN">campaign</a> against the Russians, is said to have been achieved by Albanian troops. This fierce and haughty race display a greater degree of contempt for the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, than is usual even among the most barbarous nations. The females are literally regarded as inferior animals, and treated as such; but, in the country districts, they are not confined, or veiled, as is customary in Mahometan countries. The dress of the Albanian consists of a cotton shirt, a jacket, a mantle, sandals, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>; to which is added, a large capote, or great coat, as a shelter from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Every part, except the shirt, consists of woollen. As they have usually only one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUIT">suit</a>, which they wear day and night, it soon becomes a dreadful assemblage of dirt and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-VERMIN">vermin</a>; and at length literally falls to pieces. The dress of the females is more various, and often fantastical. A singular <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> prevails among the girls, of stringing together the pieces of money which they have collected for their portion, and wearing them upon their heads. Some of them have their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> hanging <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in braids to a great length, loaded with this species of ornament. Joannina, the present capital, is beautifully situated on the banks of a small lake, enclosed within a circuit of lofty mountains. The houses, in general, are not externally either splendid or elegant; and they are built in the most irregular manner, with scarcely any approach to the form of streets. The intermixture however of gardens and trees, gives to the city a fine appearance from a distance; particularly when combined with the magnificent back-ground, which everywhere crowns the landscape. There is a considerable number of Greeks at Joannina, who display an active and intelligent character, and cultivate with ardour the different branches of science and literature. The total number of inhabitants is estimated at upwards of thirty-five thousand. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of Albania is chiefly carried on through <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTA">Arta</a>, a small city situated on a gulf of the same name, in the most southern district of the country. The principal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> however, are Greeks residing at Joannina, among whom a very active commercial spirit appears to prevail. Ali, who anxiously endeavours to promote the trade of his dominions, without however knowing the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> way, imposes great restraints on the removal of the merchants. He generally insists, that at least one member of a family should continue to reside at Joannina. The mercantile houses of this city have often branches in other countries, particularly Germany and Russia, and several of them suffered considerably by the conflagration of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOSCOW">Moscow</a>. Under the continental system of the late French ruler, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALTA">Malta</a> became the great channel for the trade of Albania, and, notwithstanding the recent political changes, may probably retain it to a certain extent. The exports consist almost entirely of unmanufactured produce. Notwithstanding its mountainous character, the fertility of its plains affords a surplus of grain, of which, upwards of fifty cargoes are sent to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, the Ionian isles, Malta, and other places. The Pasha, however has checked this commerce by the impolitic system of assuming the monopoly of it into his own hands. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">Wool</a> is exported, chiefly unmanufactured; but partly also wrought into coarse cloth. Other important <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of export are <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> of good <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>, cotton and cotton yarn, chiefly from Thessaly. Some cargoes of wood for building and fire, are annually sent to Malta. The chief imports consist of woollen cloths, used for winter coverings. For this purpose, the preference is given to a coarser and cheaper species than any that is usually manufactured in Great <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. This is supplied from Germany. Albania imports also guns, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>, hardware, coffee, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>. On the 8th of October, an annual fair is opened in the neighbourhood of Joannina, and continues for fourteen days, when the imported articles are exchanged for native commodities, which then pour in from every <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>. The reader <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> find much interesting information in regard to this country, and its present ruler, in the lately published Travels of Mr Hobhouse, and of Dr Holland. The latter resided for some time at Ali's court, where, in quality of physician, he enjoyed the privilege of a familiar intercourse with that extraordinary personage; and the anecdotes which he relates, give no small share of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> to his otherwise valuable and instructive publication.

ALCARRAZAS

Pages 463-463

a name, of Arabic origin, applied to a kind of porous earthen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARE">ware</a>, much used in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> for cooling <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. See Cooling.

ALCOOMETER

Pages 463-463
or Alkoometer, a name given by Richter to the Hydrometer with a graduated stalk. See Alcometer.

ALEUTIAN

Pages 463-470

Aleutic, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aleutsky <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">Islands</a>, (so called from the Russian word aleut, signifying a bold rock), is the name given by the Russian discoverers to a chain of small islands, situated in the Northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PACIFIC_OCEAN">Pacific Ocean</a>, and extending in an easterly <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, from the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KAMTSCHATKA">Kamtschatka</a>, in Asiatic Russia, to the promontory of Alaska, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. These islands are very shortly noticed in the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> under the head Fox Islands. According to the practice of the most recent Russian geographers, we have comprehended the whole of this archipelago under one general name, although it has been sometimes divided into three several groups: those nearest to the eastern <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of Kamtschatka being properly called Aleutian; the central <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GROUP">group</a> the Andreanofskie, or Andreonovian; and those nearest to the American promontory, the Fox Islands. The Russian geographers usually separate Behring's and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">Copper</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, which are at the western extremity of this chain, from the other parts of it, included by them under the general name of Aleutian Islands; but as there seems no good reason for this exception, it certainly would be better to comprehend the whole under one general denomination. The first voyage of discovery in this remote and dangerous archipelago was projected by <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PETER">Peter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a>, whose enterprising mind appears to have been strongly excited by the question, then much agitated, relative to the distance between the Asiatic and American Continents; the solution of which seemed to be facilitated by the recent conquest of Kamtschatka. A short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> previous to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of that monarch, which took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in 1725, he drew up instructions, with his own <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, for the conduct of an expedition, which was to be entrusted to the command of an officer named Behring, who had already made several voyages in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of Kamtschatka, by order of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CROWN">Crown</a>. In 1728, Behring set sail from the mouth of the Kamtschatka river, and coasted the eastern shores of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIBERIA">Siberia</a>, as far to the northward as latitude 67° 18', but made no discovery of the opposite Continent. In 1729, he again set sail, for the purpose of prosecuting the same enterprise, but with no better success. A third voyage was undertaken, by order of the Empress <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNA">Anna</a>, in 1741; and Behring was again selected as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the expedition; another vessel being entrusted to the command of Tschirikoff. This enterprise proved more fortunate, and led the way to all the subsequent important discoveries of the Russians in those seas; although the immediate results of the voyage, upon the whole, were not deemed commensurate with the time and expense employed in fitting out the expedition. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> object of the undertaking, however, appears to have been accomplished. Tschirikoff discovered the coast of America in the 56th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of latitude; and Behring, who was separated from his <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol5.html#article-COMPANION">companion</a> in a storm, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> it in latitude 58° 28'. On his voyage back to Kamtschatka, Behring's ship was driven on the island which now bears his name, where he soon afterwards died. The two uninhabited islands, Behring's and Copper Island, now became known to the natives of Kamtschatka, who frequently resorted thither, for the purpose of hunting sea-otters, and other animals, affording valuable furs, with which they carried on a lucrative traffic. Some of the vessels which sailed upon these expeditions were driven, by stormy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, to the south-east, by which means the group of Aleutian Islands came to be discovered. These islands seem to have been first visited in the year 1745, and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to be resorted to, for some time, by private individuals, without attracting the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a>. In the above-mentioned year a vessel, called the Eudokia, was fitted out at the expence of some private adventurers, and the command given to Michael Nevodtsikof, a native of Tobolsk. Having discovered three unknown islands, they ventured upon one of them, in order to kill sea-otters, of which they found a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. These islands were undoubtedly the nearest Aleutian Islands, and were found well inhabited. The Russians continued upon this island until the 14th September 1746, when, having incurred the enmity of the natives by their arbitrary and hostile proceedings, they put to sea, with the view of looking out for some uninhabited islands. Being overtaken, however, by a violent storm, they were driven about until the 30th October, when their vessel was wrecked upon the rocky shore of the island of Karaga, the inhabitants of which were of the Koriae tribe, and tributary to the Russian empire. From this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the zeal or avarice of individual adventurers prompted them to undertake repeated voyages to the new-discovered islands, in some of which they penetrated as far eastward as the Fox Islands, where they collected a quantity of valuable skins; but, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of their own rapacity and misconduct, they were frequently embroiled in fatal quarrels with the natives. One of the most remarkable of these voyages was that of the St Andrean and the St Natalia, fitted out by the merchant Andrean Tolstyk, which sailed from the mouth of the Kamtschatka river on the 27th September 1760, and on the 29th reached <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol4.html#article-BEHRING_S_ISLAND">Behring's Island</a>. Having been driven on shore by a violent autumnal storm, they were here obliged to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> the winter; and, after refitting, they put to sea again on the 24th <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1761. They passed by Copper Island, which lies about 150 versts from the former, and steered S.E. towards the Aleutian isles, which they did not reach before the 6th August. From thence they proceeded, on the Discovery 19th, in quest of some more distant islands, for the purpose of exacting tribute, steering their course N.E. and N.E. by E., and were driven, by a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GALE">gale</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, towards an island, where, on the 30th August, they anchored in a safe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a>. This island, they called Ayagh or Kayaka, and another, which lay at the distance of about 20 versts, Kanagra. The Russians persuaded the inhabitants of these islands to become tributary to the empress, to which they made no great objection. Four other islands were discovered in the neighbourhood; and the crew remained here, in great tranquillity, until the year 1764, but met with no great success in their hunting excursions. This group of islands, which lies somewhat to the north-west of the Fox Islands, was denominated, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the vessel which made the discovery, the Andreanofskie, or Andrenovian Isles. From the year 1758 to 1760, several vessels visited the Fox Islands, and obtained considerable cargoes of sea-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OTTER">otter</a> and fox skins. But the crews appear to have behaved with the most shameful inhumanity towards the natives; and little information was derived from these voyages, except a few particulars which --- * Mr Pinkerton appears to be mistaken when he says, that, "the nearest Aleutian Isles of the Russians, are those which we <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> Behring's and Copper." (Geog. 3d. Edit. Vol. II. p. 428.) We do not find that the term Aleutian, has ever been applied to the two islands above mentioned. That name was first given, by the early Russian discoverers, to the small group of islands, situated to the S.E. of Behring's island; and the islands composing this group, were sometimes called the nearest Aleutian isles, to distinguish them from the more easterly and remote parts of the chain. See Coxe's Russian Discoveries, chap. ii. transpired during the course of a judicial <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVESTIGATION">investigation</a> into their conduct. In 1762, four vessels sailed for the Fox Islands, of which only one returned safe to Kamtschatka. The first was the Zacharias and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>, fitted out by Kulkof and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a> of Vologda, under the command of Drusinin, with a crew of thirty-four Russians and three Kamtschadals. This vessel touched at the Aleutian Islands, and, in the beginning of September 1763, arrived at Unmak, one of the most considerable of the Fox Islands. On the 22d September they proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-UNALASHKA">Unalashka</a>, where the vessel was brought into a safe harbour. Here the crew formed themselves into hunting parties, but were soon afterwards attacked separately by the natives, and cut off, with the exception of four individuals, who, after defending themselves with astonishing courage and intrepidity, and suffering incredible hardships, succeeded in making their escape from the island in a baidar, their own vessel having been destroyed by the savages. One of these four died during the home voyage; but the other three returned safe to Kamtschatka, and gave an account of their adventures. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> vessel which sailed from Kamtschatka in 1762 was the Trinity, fitted out by the trading company of Nikiphor Trapesnikof, a merchant of Irkutsk, under the command of Ivan Korovin, and manned with thirty-eight Russians and six Kamtschadals. In the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of October they <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> before the south side of Behring's Island, where they resolved to winter, on account of the late season of the year. On the 1st of August 1763, Korovin sailed from Behring's Island, in company with Dennis Medvedef, who commanded a vessel fitted out by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a> Protassof, merchant of Tiumen. On the 15th the former vessel made Unalashka, and Medvedef reached Unmak. After having reconnoitred the coast, and received hostages from the Toigons, or Chiefs, Korovin sent out several hunting parties; but the natives soon began to exhibit hostile intentions, and three Kamtschadals, belonging to Kulkof's ship, arrived with accounts of the destruction of that vessel, and the massacre of the crew. On the 10th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DECEMBER">December</a>, the savages assembled in large bodies, and invested the hut which the Russians had constructed, and continually annoyed them with their darts. Korovin, finding himself thus harassed by the natives, ordered the hut to be destroyed, and retired to his vessel, which was removed to the distance of an hundred yards from the beach, where they lay at anchor from the 5th <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> to the 26th April 1764. Here the natives attempted to surprise the vessel; but Korovin, having been warned of their approach, compelled them to retreat. On the 26th April, Korovin sailed from Unalashka, and, after being driven about by contrary winds, the vessel was at length stranded, on the 28th, in a bay of the Island of Unmak. Having got on shore, the crew attempted to secure themselves between their baidar and some empty barrels, with the sails spread over them in the form of a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENT">tent</a>. Next morning, before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, they were surprised by a large body of the natives, who attacked them with their darts, and wounded every one of the crew. Korovin, however, sailed out, in company with four Russians, and put the savages to flight; although he and his party were so severely wounded, that they had scarcely sufficient strength to return to the tent. During the night, the vessel was dashed to pieces by the storm. On the 30th of April, they were again attacked by the natives, who, however, were soon put to flight by the fire of the Russians. On the 21st of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, Korovin, with the remainder of his crew, which was now reduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of twelve persons, including six Kamtschadals, put to sea in a baidar; and, having landed upon another <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the same island, they discovered the remains of a vessel which had been burnt, and, at a small distance, a deserted Russian dwelling, containing twenty dead bodies in their clothes; among which they recognized several of those individuals who had sailed in Protassof's vessel, and distinguished, among the rest, the commander Medvedef. Korovin afterwards joined Glottof's vessel, (of whose proceedings we shall immediately give some account), which he quitted in the month of April 1765, and went over, with five other Russians, to Soloviof, with whom he returned, the following year, to Kamtschatka. The third voyage from Kamtschatka in 1762, and Voyage of the most fortunate and most remarkable of the whole, Stephen Glottof, in was that of the Andrean and Natalia, which was fitted out by Terenty Tsebneffskoi and Company, under the command of Stephen Glottof, an experienced and skillful seaman of Yarensk. This vessel sailed on the 1st October, with a crew of thirty-eight Russians and eight Kamtschadals. Having wintered at Copper Island, they set sail from thence on the 26th July 1763, and steered for the Fox Islands. In consequence of storms and contrary winds, they were thirty days on the voyage to Unmak, where they arrived on the 24th August, and, without dropping anchor, sailed farther in quest of new islands, of which they passed eight contiguous to each other, and separated by straits from 20 to 100 versts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Glottof, however, did not <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> until he reached the most eastward of these islands, called by the inhabitants Kadyak. Here, and in the neighbouring islands, they passed the winter, and collected a considerable quantity of furs; but as the conduct of the natives, at first decidedly hostile, was always suspicious, Glottof did not think it prudent to prolong his stay; and accordingly, having taken on board all the peltry and stores, he left Kadyak on the 24th May 1764, and sailed for Unmak, where he arrived on the 3d July. He remained here two years, sending out hunting parties through the islands of Unmak and Unalashka, and commenced his voyage homewards in the month of July 1766. In the month of August he arrived safe in Kamtschatka river with a rich cargo. Soloviof, to whose voyage we have already alluded, sailed from Kamtschatka on the 25th of Au- * This was the fourth vessel which sailed in 1762; but, as the whole crew were massacred by the natives, we have no distinct account of the voyage. gust 1764, in a ship called the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, fitted out by Jacob Ulednikof and Company, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of Irkutsk. This vessel reached Unalashka on the 17th September, where Soloviof passed two winters; and having succeeded, notwithstanding the continual hostility of the natives, in collecting a considerable cargo of peltry, he returned to Kamtschatka in the month of July 1766. Having thus traced an outline of the gradual progress of early discovery in this archipelago, it seems unnecessary to proceed with an enumeration of the subsequent voyages performed by private individuals. These were undertaken merely for commercial purposes; the accounts brought home by the adventurers were generally imperfect and incorrect; and rather tended to excite than to gratify the curiosity of those who might be desirous of obtaining more accurate and more ample information. We shall, therefore, now turn to the conduct of those expeditions, which were fitted out by the State for the express purpose of discovery. In the year 1768, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Krenitzin and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEUTENANT">Lieutenant</a> Levashof sailed from the mouth of the Kamtschatka river, by order of the Empress Catharine, to examine the chain of Aleutian Islands. This <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> they accordingly executed very carefully, having surveyed the whole of this archipelago, from Behring's Island to the promontory of Alaska; and, after spending the winter among the Fox Islands, they returned to Kamtschatka in the autumn of 1769. But our great navigator, Captain Cook, communicated more accurate scientific information respecting these islands, as well as the coasts of the two continents, than all the previous voyages of the Russian discoverers had afforded. During his third and last voyage, in the year 1778, he surveyed the eastern portion of this archipelago, accurately determined the positions of some of the most remarkable islands, and corrected many errors of former navigators. In the year 1785, a fresh expedition was set on foot by the Russian government, the command of which was entrusted to Captain Billings, an English naval officer in the Russian <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>, who had accompanied Captain Cook in his last celebrated voyage to the Pacific Ocean. This expedition appears to have been suggested by Mr Coxe, who was at that time at St Petersburg, and whose Account of the Russian Discoveries between <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> and America, had already attracted the attention of the Russian government. During this voyage, which was not completed until the year 1796, Captains Billings and Sarytschef explored the whole chain of the Aleutian islands, particularly that part of it which had been visited by Captain Cook, and some parts of the adjacent western coast of America. Ample details of the conduct of this expedition have been published in the narratives of Martin Sauer, who officiated as secretary to Captain Billings, and of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ADMIRAL">Admiral</a> Sarytschef. Some years after the termination of the expedition under Captain Billings, the attention of the Russian American Company was turned towards the best means of supplying their settlements on the north-west coast of America with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> and stores of all kinds; and it was resolved to try whether the Aleutian conveyance by sea would not answer the purpose better, than the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> and tedious journey by land to Ochotsk. With the view of ascertaining the practicability of the project, Captain Krusenstern, an experienced Russian naval officer, who had served for a long period in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">Navy</a>, suggested the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of an expedition from <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CRONSTADT">Cronstadt</a>, round <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">Horn</a>, to the Aleutian Islands and the north-west coast of America. This plan was approved of by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Romanzof, the Minister of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, and Admiral Mordwinof, Minister of the Marine, and obtained the sanction of his Imperial Majesty. Two vessels, called by the Russians the Nadeshda and the Neva, were accordingly purchased in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a> for the voyage. The command of the expedition was intrusted to Captain Krusenstern, the original author of the plan; and Captain Lisiansky was appointed to the Neva. These two vessels accordingly sailed in company from Cronstadt, in the month of August 1803, and, after a short stay at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>, proceeded to the Brazils; from whence they sailed round Cape Horn to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a> Islands. Here they separated; the Nadeshda being ordered on a distinct mission to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAPAN">Japan</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; while Captain Lisiansky, in the Neva, proceeded to Kadyak and the American settlements. Of this voyage, very full and interesting accounts have been lately published by Captains Krusenstern and Lisiansky, and by Dr Langsdorff, who accompanied the expedition in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> of physician. From the ample sources of information, to which we have alluded in the foregoing narrative, we shall now proceed to exhibit an enumeration and general <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the islands composing this singular chain, which appears to be a prolongation of either continent. We shall begin with the more westerly part of the chain, consisting of those islands which <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LIE">lie</a> nearest to Kamtschatka, and proceed eastwards to the American promontory. The first is Commodore's or Behring's Island, situate (according to Cook's reckoning), in 55° of latitude, and 6° of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONGITUDE">longitude</a> from the harbour of Petropaulowska in the bay of Awatska. It is from 70 to 80 versts long, and stretches from north-west to south-east. Ten leagues from the south-east point of this island, in the direction of east by south, or east-south-east, lies Mednoi Ostroff, or Copper Island, so called from large masses of native copper being found upon the beach. To the south-east of Copper Island lie three small islands, Attak, or Attoo, Semitshi, and Agattoo, called by the Russians Plishnic Ostrova, or the nearest Aleutian Islands. Of these Attak is the largest; it is nearly of the same shape as Behring's Island, but rather more extensive, stretching from west to east to the length of 18 leagues. These islands are situate between 54° and 55° of north latitude. Attak has two harbours, one of which lies on the southern coast. From the eastern extremity of the Aleutian Islands, properly so called, another group runs, south-eastward, continuing the chain as far as the western extremity of the Fox Islands. These are called the Andreanofskie Islands; but we have less accurate information respecting this central part of the chain, than regarding the eastern and western groups. They are said to lie within the 52d and 54th degree of north latitude, to be of inconsiderable <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> or importance, and, therefore, seldom visited by recent navigators. The most remarkable are, Takavangha, which has in its centre, near the northern coast, a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> mountain; Kanaghi, or Kanaga, likewise with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> smoking mountain; Ayag, which has a number of good bays and anchoring-places; and Tshetchina, on which a high <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> mountain overtops the rest, which apparently is an extinct volcano, as there are still hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> on this island. Atshak, or Atchka, and Amlac, are also usually reckoned among the number of the Andreonovian isles. The former greatly resembles Copper Island, and is provided with a commodious harbour. By far the most important and best explored portion of this archipelago is the most easterly group, called by the Russians Lysic Ostrovo, or the Fox Islands. Of these islands the most considerable are, Umnak, Unalashka, or Oonalashka; and Unimak; the last of which is separated by a narrow strait from the promontory of Alaska. Beyond these, to the north-east, lies the large island of Kadyak, or Kodiak, which is generally included among the group called Schumagin's Islands. The whole of the islands composing this chain are bare and mountainous; their coasts are rocky and surrounded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAKERS">breakers</a>, which renders the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> of those seas exceedingly dangerous. The land rises immediately from the coasts to steep bald <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, gradually ascending higher behind each other, and assuming the appearance of chains of mountains, with a direction lengthwise of the island. Springs take their rise at the bottom of the mountains, and either flow in broad and rapid streams into the neighbouring sea, or, collecting in the rocky vales and glens, form ample <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, which send off their superfluous waters, by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>, into the adjacent bays. These islands bear evident marks of volcanic formation; and several of them have still <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> volcanoes, which continually emit <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, and sometimes flames. No traces of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> have been discovered on these islands; but carnoles and sardonyxes are brought from thence. Their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is said to be similar to that of Kamtschatka; and affords the same kinds of edible wild berries and roots; excepting some few vegetables which seem to be of foreign origin. No wood of any considerable growth has been perceived upon any of these islands, except a very small quantity, on Unalashka. The land animals are bears, wolves, river-otters, river-beavers, and ermines. The sea-otter, so valuable on account of its skin, is frequently caught; but the number of these animals, it is believed, is much diminished of late. On the Fox Islands they have a great variety of foxes, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, grey, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a>. The sea abounds with all sorts of seals, dolphins, and whales; sea-lions and porpoises are rare, and sea-cows not at all to be seen. Salmon are caught in great abundance and variety; and halibut of an immense size are frequently taken. The winter upon these islands is tolerably mild, but the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is equally short and unpleasant. The inhabitants are pretty numerous, and tributary to Russia, from whence vessels are sent out, and establishments formed upon these islands, on account of the very profitable chace of sea-otters and foxes. Unalashka, one of the largest of the Fox Islands, Island of was visited by Captain Cook during his last voyage, and seems to merit particular notice. This island stretches from north-east to south-west, and is from 70 to 80 versts in length, but of very unequal breadth. On the north and north-east side there are many bays and creeks, in some of which are very secure harbours for vessels. A part of the southwest shore consists of very high, steep, inaccessible cliffs; and another part has remained hitherto wholly unexplored. The whole island consists of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> of rocks, covered only with a very thin coat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>; the hills are of very unequal height, and are intersected by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> valleys, the soil of which is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> argillaceous, or an earth which appears washed <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the hills. In the lower valleys there is great abundance of grass, which would furnish very good food for cattle; indeed Captain Cook was of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that cattle might subsist at Unalashka all the year round, without being housed; and the soil, in many places, appeared capable of producing grain, roots, and vegetables. But the Russian traders, and the natives, seem satisfied with what <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> brings forth. No wood grows on this and the neighbouring islands; only low bushes and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DWARF">dwarf</a>-birch, willow, and alder. For all the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> used for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, &c., they are indebted to the sea, which wafts it to their shores from the adjacent continent of America. The inhabitants are rather low of stature, but plump and well shaped; with the Natives, short necks, swarthy chubby faces, black eyes, small beards, and long, straight, black <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, which the men wear loose behind, and cut before, but the women tie up in a bunch. With regard to their character, Captain Cook describes them as, to all appearance, the most inoffensive people he ever met with, and perfect patterns of honesty. But, according to the accounts of the first discoverers, this does not seem to have been their original disposition; and recent travellers have observed, that although generally kind-hearted and peaceable, yet, when roused to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGER">anger</a>, they become exceedingly malevolent, and indifferent to all danger, even to death itself. The clothing of the men and women Dress, is nearly the same, and consists of a sort of frock or shirt, called parka, fastened round the neck with a broad stiff collar, and descending below the knee. These garments are made of the skins of seals, prepared in a manner peculiar to themselves, and sewed together very ingeniously. Though simple in their form, they are ornamented in a variety of ways; with glass beads; beaks of sea parrots; long white goat's hair, brought from Siberia, or small red feathers. Over the frock, the men sometimes bear a kamleika, or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>-garment. This is made of gut, which is <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a>; and has a hood to it, which draws over the head, and is tied under the chin. When on shore, the men wear boots, made of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEAL">seal</a>'s skin; and they all have a kind of oval snouted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, made of wood, with a rim to admit the head. These caps are dyed with green and other Aleutian Islands. colours, and are very fancifully ornamented with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> figures, carved from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> of the sea-cow, with glass or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> beads, and with the bristles from the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> of the sea-lion. They make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of no paint; <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TATTOOING">tattooing</a> was formerly very much in use among them, particularly among the women; but their intercourse with the Russians has rather brought this practice into disrepute. Both men and women, particularly the latter, bore the under lip, and insert pieces of bone or other ornaments; but this practice has also decreased of late. The women, for the most part, go barefooted; they wear bracelets of glass beads <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> above the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WRIST">wrist</a> and ankle-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, and are very fond of rings upon their fingers. The principal food of these islanders consists of fish, sea-animals, birds, roots and berries. They dry large quantities of fish in summer, which they lay up in small huts for winter use; and roots and berries are also preserved for the same time of scarcity. Among the fish, the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> and most abundant are several sorts of salmon, cod, herrings, and halibut. The last is the most esteemed, and is sometimes caught of an enormous size. The fat of the whale is also a favourite <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of food; when it grows old and rancid, it serves to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> and warm their houses. They eat almost everything raw; but of late, they have learnt some simple modes of cookery from the Russians. Vegetable food does not appear to be held in much esteem by the Unalashkans. That sweet plant, the Siberian parsnip, (*Heracleum Sibiricum*), is but little eaten, any more than the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the *Saranna*, or Kamtschadale lily. Berries of an eatable quality abound; such as brambleberries, cranberries, huckleberries, heath-berries, and several others. Of late, the Russians have begun to plant potatoes, which succeed extremely well, and are much liked by the people. The habitations of the Unalashkans are holes dug in the earth, covered with a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROOF">roof</a>, over which they throw grass and earth; so that a village has the appearance of an European <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>-yard full of graves. The entrance into these huts is from the roof; some of the largest, however, which are inhabited by the Russians, have a low door in the side. The light is also admitted by the roof, through an opening or window covered over with seal's entrails, or dried fish-skin. Several divisions are made within, by means of seal-skins or straw-mats, which separate the apartments of the different families that occupy the habitation. Their <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSEHOLD">household</a>-furniture consists of bowls, spoons, buckets, piggins or cans, matted baskets, and perhaps a Russian kettle or pot. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> and the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>, or rather a small flat piece of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, made like an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADZE">adze</a>, by fitting it into a crooked wooden handle, are the only iron tools found amongst them. Yet all their instruments and utensils are made with the greatest neatness, and the most exact symmetry. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, with which they sew their clothes and embroider, are made of the wing-bone of the gull, with a very nice cut round the thicker end, instead of an eye, to which they tie the thread so skilfully, that it follows the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> without any obstruction. Their thread is made of the sinews of the seal, the fibres of which they split to the thickness which each sort of work requires. All sewing is performed by the women; they are the tailors, shoemakers, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>-builders, or boat-coverers. At their leisure hours, particularly in long winter evenings, they make fine mats, little baskets, and pocket-books of straw, that are both beautiful and strong. Indeed, Captain Cook observes, there is a neatness and perfection in most of their work, that shows they neither want ingenuity nor perseverance. Their houses have no fire-place, but are heated, as Use of Fire well as lighted, by lamps. These are made of a flat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, hollowed on one side like a plate; in the hollow part they put the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, mixed with a little dry grass, which serves the purpose of a wick. They produce fire both by collision and by attrition; the former by striking two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> one against another, of producing one of them being previously rubbed with brimstone. The latter method is with two pieces of wood; one of which is a pointed stick, and the other a flat piece. The pointed end of the stick they press upon the other, whirling it nimbly round as a drill; thus producing fire in a few minutes. The principal occupations of the Aleutians, are Occupations <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> and hunting, and preparing the implements necessary for both. Their *baidars*, *baidarkas*, or boats, resemble the canoes of other savages. They consist of a skeleton of wood, over which is stretched a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> covering made of seals' skins. The boats of the Unalashkans are much superior in point of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> to those of any of the other islands; some of them appear so transparent that one might trace the formation of the inside, and the manner in which the rower sits. In their form, they are long and narrow, and commonly hold only one person; sometimes they are made to hold two, and very rarely three; each person sitting in a round hole just fitted to the size of the body. The whole canoe is so extremely light, even when sodden with water, that it may be carried with ease in one hand. They are impelled by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> paddles, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> or eight feet long, which are managed with great dexterity. Experienced navigators <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> sometimes venture out a considerable way to sea in these boats, even in very stormy weather. The Darts used darts, or javelins, with which they kill their <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAME">game</a>, in Hunting, are formed with the same neatness as their other instruments, and adapted with the greatest judgment to the different objects of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHASE">chase</a>. For land animals, a single barbed point; for birds, three <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of light bone, spread, and barbed; for seals, &c., they use a false point, inserted in a socket at the end of the dart, which parts on the least effort of the animal to dive, remaining in its body. A string of considerable length is fastened to this barbed point, and twisted round the wooden part of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVELIN">javelin</a>. This serves as a float to <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> them to the seal, which, having the stick to drag after it, soon tires, and becomes an easy prey. These darts are not <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> from Curies no bow, but slung from a small plank, about 18 inches long and two inches broad. In order that the weapon may be held the faster, they have a sort of handle at the lower end, and an opening through which the fore-finger is thrust. At the other end is a small channel, into which the javelin fits with a little knob, which serves to retain it. When the javelin is to be thrown, the plank is held horizontally, and the aim being taken, the weapon is directed by the middle finger and thumb. This is done with so much dexterity, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> given to it is so powerful and so rapid, that the object aimed at is rarely missed; even whales are killed without any other weapon. Their favourite amusement appears to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>; in which, however, they do not seem to exhibit any particular exertion of strength, or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of elegance; the only motion being a sort of hop, the performer scarcely moving from the place he first takes up. Their music is exceedingly rude, consisting of a small drum or tambour, and a rattle made of the bladder of a sea-dog, filled with peas or small pebbles. In their leisure hours, they amuse themselves with making these little drums and rattles, which are frequently ornamented with a good <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of ingenuity and elegance; and with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> out from the teeth of the sea-cow, small figures of men, fish, sea-otters, and other objects, in a manner that appears very extraordinary, considering that the sea-cow's teeth are much harder than ivory, and that they have no proper tools to work with. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of these Islanders, like that of most uncivilized nations, consists in superstitious observances, and a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> in charms. Many of them have been baptized, and are nominally professors of the Greek <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>; of which, however, they understand nothing more than making the sign of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a>. They have no <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>; every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may have as many wives as he can conveniently maintain; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his means decrease, he sends first one, then another back to their parents; and these women become perfectly at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to look out for other husbands. Sometimes the same woman lives with two husbands; and it is not uncommon for men to sell or <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> wives. Boys, if they happen to be very handsome, are often brought up entirely in the manner of girls; instructed in the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> blandishment; and used as concubines. This shocking, unnatural, and immoral practice, has prevailed here even from the remotest times. Such men are known under the name of schopans. The bodies of the dead, especially of the men, were formerly interred in places set apart for the purpose, and with particular ceremonies. Their best javelins and clothes, with a portion of train-oil and other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of food, were laid with them in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAVE">grave</a>; and sometimes even slaves of both sexes were slaughtered upon the occasion. These customs are now, however, entirely laid aside. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Unalashka, and the neighbouring islands, appears to have been formerly considerable, amounting to several thousands. In 1790, Sarytcheff reckoned it at 1300. According to the most recent accounts, it does not appear to amount to more than 300. This rapid depopulation is ascribed partly to the practice of sending the best hunters from hence to a distance, to chase the large sea-otters, few of whom ever return again to their families; and partly to the state of oppression under which the natives live, and the change which has taken place in their modes of living. Captain Cook seems to consider the natives of these Islands as originally of the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> with the Greenlanders and Esquimaux. When first discovered by the Russians, they were under the government of Toigons, or chiefs, who, however, possessed little superior distinction or <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a>, and had no revenue. At present they are all subject to the government of the Russian settlers. Throughout the whole of the Aleutian Islands, on the Russian settlement of Kadyak, and the western coast of America, the Russians have formed settlements for the purpose of hunting, and collecting furs; with which they carry on a lucrative commerce, particularly with the Chinese. The most valuable fur is that of the sea-otter; an animal which has now become rare on these islands, in consequence of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> eagerness with which they have been hunted and killed. Besides the sea-otter, there are numbers of foxes, especially on the Fox Islands. The black foxes found on these islands are not so valuable as those of Siberia. The Arctic, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a> fox, called also the rock fox, and the blue fox, from the natural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the fur, which is of a bluish grey, is very common. From the discovery of these islands by Behring and Tschelikoff, in 1741, the fur-trade was carried on for a long period entirely by private adventurers; and appears to have been productive of great abuses. The natives were frequently treated in the most cruel and barbarous manner; and the keenness displayed by these rapacious hunters, threatened to extirpate the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of animals upon which the trade depended. Convinced of the extreme <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of putting a stop to this destructive plan of proceeding, Schelikoff, an intelligent Russian merchant, took considerable pains to unite the different partakers of this trade into a company, in order that it might be conducted with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and precaution, upon some plan that might prove advantageous to all parties. In 1785, he succeeded in joining company with the Golikoffs. They increased their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and fitted out several ships, which the enterprising Schelikoff commanded in person. Factories, protected by forts, were established in almost all the Aleutian islands, as far eastward as Kadyak; and, during several years, they continued this lucrative trade in conjunction, by which they acquired considerable wealth. The success of this connection induced several merchants to unite like Schelikoff and the Golikoffs; and, in this manner, was laid the foundation of the present Russian American Company. The irregular manner, however, in which the trade was still carried on, and the cruelty which was frequently exercised by the Russian merchants towards the natives of the islands, drew upon them great and well-founded censure; insomuch, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a> Paul determined to put an end to the company and the trade at the same time. This determination would have infallibly been carried into effect, but for the interference of M. Von Resanoff, who had married Schelikoff's <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, and was personally interested in the successful continuance of the American Company. In consequence of his active interposition, the new established company was formally confirmed, in 1799, with considerable privileges. On the accession of the present Emperor, his Majesty interested himself very much in behalf of the company, of which he became a member, and thus induced many of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> to follow his example; and by means of the active superintendence of the minister, Count Romanzoff, and the Commer- VOL. I. PART I. cial Counsellor Benedict Cramer; this branch of the Russian commerce has undergone several advantageous changes. But, according to the accounts of recent observers, many abuses still exist which loudly call for correction. The miserable situation of the Proviščeniks, or fur-collectors, themselves the slaves of the company's agents, and exercising, in their turn, the most oppressive tyranny over the wretched Aleutians, has been represented by several eye-witnesses in the most deplorable colours. It is to be hoped, that these representations may attract the serious attention of the Russian Government; and that the information which the late voyages have brought to light, with regard to the evils connected with the present system of management, may <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>, tending at once to the better regulation of the trade, and to the amelioration of the condition of those remote settlements. They who are desirous of obtaining more ample information on the subject of this article, may consult the following works: Müller's Sammlung Russischer Geschichte; particularly the third volume. Neue Nachrichten von denen neuentdeckten Insulae in der See zwischen Asia und America, &c. verfasset von J. L. S.—Hamburgh and Leipsic, 1776. Coxe's Account of the Russian Discoveries. Tooke's View of the Russian Empire. The Voyages and Travels of Billings; Sarytcheff; Cooke; Meares; Dixon; Vancouver; La Peyrouse; Mackenzie; Krusenstern; Lisiansky; and Dr Langsdorff. (n.)

ALFARABIIUS

Pages 470-470

a celebrated Eastern <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> of the tenth century, was born, in what year is not known, at Farab, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASIA_MINOR"><a class="</a>xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, now called Othrar. He studied for sometime at <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, then the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> seat of learning; and afterwards travelled, in order to form an acquaintance with the learned of other countries. A <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> revolution of sentiment in regard to letters, had taken <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, in the preceding century, among the followers of Mahomet. The Commanders of the Faithful had become the patrons and cultivators, instead of the scourgings and contemners, of science and literature. Knowledge found her only sanctuary under the successors of those rulers who had sought to extinguish every ray of intellectual <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, by means of the destruction of the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol13.html#article-LIBRARIES">libraries</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALEXANDRIA">Alexandria</a>. Instead of proscribing every book as useless but the Koran, some of these rulers carried their zeal in the cause of learning so far, as to make the acquisition of Greek <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUSCRIPTS">manuscripts</a> an object of negotiation, in their treaties with the Emperors of Constantinople. Under the Caliphs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Abbas, men of learning were raised to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of favour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, which has never been enjoyed by that class, under the sovereigns of any other <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, in any <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of the world. The munificence which shone forth with so much lustre in the supreme depositaries of power, was widely emulated among the inferior rulers and governors; and "this emulation," to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> the words of Gibbon, "diffused the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and the rewards of science, from Samarcan and Bochara, to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEZ">Fez</a> and Cordova." Every little <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> had its circle of men of letters, who were always admitted to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCE">Prince</a>, and for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> liberally supported by his bounty. Thus, when Alfarabius, after he had finished his travels, came to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> at Damas, he was received with Alfarabian open arms by its sovereign, who bestowed upon him a pension, which he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to enjoy till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in the year 950. But to <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> the notice of princes, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> to acquire wealth, formed none of the aims of this philosopher. He is said to have led a very retired and ascetic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, rather contemning than seeking after the good things of the world. "He constantly slept, even during winter, upon straw; his countenance was always sorrowful, and he found no consolation in anything but <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>." (Enfield's Hist. of Philosophy, B.v.c.l.) His works were numerous, and very various in their subjects; his speculations seem, indeed, from the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his writings, to have embraced the whole circle of the sciences. He is particularly deserving of notice, as having been perhaps the first compiler of an Encyclopedia. Such is the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of one of his works, of which there is a copy in manuscript, in the library of the Escorial. It contains, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> notice of it given in Casiri's valuable account of the Arabic Manuscripts in that collection, a clear and comprehensive <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> and compendium of all the Arts and Sciences; and it appears to have been regarded in the East as the most valuable of Alfarabius's compositions. It would have been agreeable to the lovers of literary <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> to have possessed some more detailed view of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a>, and contents of an Encyclopedia, written by an Arabian, so many centuries before any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> was thought of in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. Next to this in estimation appears to have been his treatise on Music; in which he is said to have applied the principles of physics to correct the errors of musical theorists, and to regulate the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of musical instruments. (Biog. Universelle, Tom. I.) Casiri gives a complete list of his writings; but it is too <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> to be copied in this place. (See Bibl. Arabico-Hispana Escorialensis, Tom. I.) Some of his pieces were published, in the Latin tongue, at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, in 1638, under the title of Opuscula Varia Alfarabii.

ALFERGAN

Pages 470-471
or ALFRAGAN, an Arabian astronomer, who lived under the reign of the Caliph Almanon, and who, on account of his skill in calculation, was surnamed the Calculator. He wrote an Introduction to Astronomy, which contains little that is original, being chiefly compiled from the Almagest of Ptolemy. He was also the author of a treatise on Dials, and of an account of the construction and use of the Astrolabe. These two pieces still remain in manuscript; but there have been three different Latin translations published of his astronomical work. The first, by Joannes Hispalensis, was published at Ferrara in 1493. This translation was afterwards reprinted at Nuremberg in 1537, with a preface by Melanchton. The second was the work of John Christman, and was published at Frankfort in 1590. The third, and the most esteemed of these translations, was by Golius, Professor of Mathematics and Oriental Languages at Leyden. It was published at Amsterdam in 1669, accompanied with the Arabic text, and with notes by Golius, which are extremely curious. But these notes extend no farther than the ninth chapter, as the author did not live to complete Alfieri's work itself contains thirty chapters, all of which are very short.

ALFIERI

Pages 471-473

chiefly celebrated as the author who raised the Italian tragic drama from its previous state of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEGRADATION">degradation</a>, was born on the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1749, at the town of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTI">Asti</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIEDMONT">Piedmont</a>. He lost his father in early infancy; but he <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to reside with his mother, who married a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, till his tenth year, when he was placed at the academy of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURIN">Turin</a>. After he had passed a twelvemonth at the academy, he went on a short visit to a relation who dwelt at Comi, and during his stay there, he made his first poetical attempt in a sonnet chiefly borrowed from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> in Ariosto and Metastasio, the only poets he had at that time read. When thirteen years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> he was induced to commence the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of civil and canonical <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but the attempt only served to disgust him with every <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of application, and to increase his relish for the perusal of French romances. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his uncle, who had hitherto taken some <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and conduct, he was left, at the age of fourteen, to enjoy without control his vast paternal inheritance, augmented by the recent accession of his uncle's fortune. He now began to attend the riding-school, where he acquired that rage for horses, and equestrian <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, which continued to be one of his strongest passions till the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of his existence. After some time spent in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> fits of extravagant dissipation, and ill-directed study, he was seized with a desire of travelling; and having obtained permission from the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KING">king</a>, he departed, in 1766, under the care of an English preceptor. Restless and unquiet, he posted with the utmost rapidity through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and his improvement was such as was to be expected from his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of travelling and his previous habits. Dissatisfied with himself, he felt as little relish for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECTACLES">spectacles</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> entertainments as for literature; and was as little amused by the gaiety of a carnival at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>, as he was impressed by the remains of antiquity at Rome, or the exhibitions of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> art at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>. This indifference and insensibility did not, however, arise from defect of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> or the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> powers of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, but from the want of some serious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PASSION">passion</a>, or some enabling or praiseworthy pursuit. Hoping to find in foreign countries some relief from the tedium and ennui with which he was oppressed, and being anxious to become acquainted with the French <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEATRE">Theatre</a>, he proceeded to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; but his feelings were only those of disgust or indifference for the dramas which he <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> represented in that <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. He seems, indeed, to have been completely dissatisfied with everything he witnessed in France, and contracted a dislike to its people, which his intercourse in future years rather contributed to augment than diminish. In <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> he became deeply enamoured of a married lady, who returned his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, but who was soon obliged to accompany her husband to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWITZERLAND">Switzerland</a>. Alfieri, whose feelings were of the most impetuous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, was in despair at this separation, and returned to his own <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> in the utmost anguish and despondency of mind. While under this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEPRESSION">depression</a> of spirits, he was induced to seek alleviation from works of literature; and the perusal of Plutarch's Lives, which he read with profound <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMOTION">emotion</a>, inspired him with an enthusiastic passion for freedom and independence. Under the influence of this rage for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> he recommenced his travels; and his only gratification, in the absence of freedom among the Continental States, appears to have been derived from contemplating the wild and sterile regions of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>; where gloomy forests, <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and precipices, conspired to excite those sublime and melancholy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> which were congenial to his disposition. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">Human</a> manners and human institutions he seems invariably to have surveyed with an eye of passion or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>, instead of viewing them with the calmness of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, who meditates how they may be rectified, or what <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LESSONS">lessons</a> may be drawn from them. In every country his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> felt as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> confined by the bonds of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a>; he everywhere panted for something more free in governments, more elevated in sentiment, more devoted in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, and more perfect in friendship. In search of this ideal world, he posted through various countries, more with the rapidity of a courier, than of one who travels for amusement or instruction. During a journey to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, he engaged in an intrigue with a married lady of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>; and having been detected, the publicity of a rencontre with the injured husband, and of a divorce, which followed, united to the knowledge he now acquired of the infamous character of the woman, to whom he was ardently attached, rendered it expedient and desirable for him to quit England. He then visited <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, where he became acquainted with the Abbé Caluso, who remained through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> the most attached and estimable friend he ever possessed. In 1772, Alfieri returned to Turin, where he again became enamoured of a lady, whom he loved with his usual ardour; and who seems to have been as undeserving of a sincere attachment as those he had hitherto adored. In the course of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> attendance on his mistress, during a malady with which she was afflicted, he one <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIALOGUE">dialogue</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of a drama, which he left at this lady's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. About a year after, on a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> taking <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between them, this piece was returned to him. Having then retouched and extended it to five acts, it was performed at Turin in 1775, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Cleopatra, whose amours had always been a favourite subject with Italian dramatists. From this moment, Alfieri was seized with an immeasurable thirst of theatrical fame, and the remainder of his life was devoted to its attainment. His two first tragedies, Filippo and Polinice, were originally written in French prose; and when he came to versify them in Italian, he found that, from his Lombard origin, and long intercourse with foreigners, he expressed himself with febleness and inaccuracy. Accordingly, with the view of improving his Italian style, he went to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and, during an alternate residence at Florence and Siena, he completed his Filippo and Polinice, and conceived the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of various other dramas. While thus employed, he became acquainted with the Countess <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ALBANY">Albany</a>, who then resided with her husband at Florence. For her he formed an attachment, which, if less violent Alfieri than his former loves, appears to have been more permanent. With this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> to remain at Florence, he could not endure the chains by which his vast possessions bound him to Piedmont. He therefore resigned his whole <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> to his sister, the Countess Cumiana, reserving an annuity, which scarcely amounted to a half of his original revenues. At this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the Countess Albany, urged by the ill-treatment she received from her husband, sought refuge in Rome, where she at length received permission from the Pope to live apart from her tormentor. Alfieri followed the Countess to that capital, where he completed fourteen tragedies, four of which were now for the first time printed at <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SIENNA">Sienna</a>. At length, however, it was thought proper, that, by leaving Rome, he should remove the aspersions which had been thrown on the object of his affections. During the year 1783, he therefore travelled through different states of Italy, and published six additional tragedies.
