As this expedition is performed by water, it is escorted by a number of the regents of the districts in their barges, which they are obliged to equip at their own expense. The governor generally sets out in the middle of October, attended by all the residents of those districts under the immediate management of the supreme government. As he proceeds, he calls on the attendance of all the principal people of the district through which he passes. He makes the tour in this manner of his whole dominions, continuing to increase his train of attendants, until, having made the complete circuit of the island, he returns to his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>. His annual cavalcade is much complained of, on account of the numerous exactions to which it gives rise. In gathering the cloves, each labourer brings the quantity which he gathers to a weigh-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where the name of the person, together with the quantity delivered, is regularly noted. But, unless the cloves are thoroughly dried, the full weight is not always admitted. There must be an allowance for wastage, which is entirely at the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-DISCRETION">discretion</a> of the receiving officer, and under this pretence the unprotected inhabitants are exposed to numerous frauds. The price at which cloves are received by the State is 4s. 8d. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>. But this price is merely nominal, in consequence of large deductions being subsequently made on various accounts. Of these the principal is an allowance of 20 per cent. on the weight of the cloves, for the benefit of the governor, and the other servants of the Company; besides which, there are other deductions for the regent and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> magistrates of the district, and the labourer's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a> are also paid out of the price allowed by the State. The annual produce of cloves is estimated at 600,000 lb., from which a deduction of one-fifth, or twenty per cent., amounts to 120,000 lb.; and the tribute thus levied is portioned out among the residents and members of the executive government, according to their respective ranks. The produce of cloves is apt to vary, however, according as the season is favourable or otherwise. For six years, ending 1791, the average quantity of cloves imported into <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a> amounted to 597,617 lbs., and were sold for a sum equal to L. 155,129; besides which, considerable quantities are annually sent to various parts of India, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>; the exact amount of which it is impossible to ascertain. When the island was taken possession of by the British in 1796, there were in store 515,940 lbs. of cloves. The quantity imported by the English East India Company after the conquest of the island by Britain, was, in the years 1803, 1804, 1805, respectively, 49,441; 127,866; 179,507 lbs, which were sold for L. 8,789; L. 19,994; L. 27,912. The despotism under which this fine island is oppressed, is sufficiently implied in the monopoly of its produce for the state, and in the severe and sanguinary laws which are found necessary to prevent contraband trade. If the government were to deal fairly with its subjects, the temptation to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to other countries with this produce would be much diminished; and, in proportion to the severity of the laws established against such an intercourse, we may, therefore, fairly estimate the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of the fraud practised upon the inhabitants by their mercantile despots. Monopoly, besides being in itself an odious abuse, is an impure source from which other abuses naturally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; and in Amboyna, accordingly, we find that, as the produce of the inhabitants is engrossed by the State at an undervalue, they are upon the same principle forced to purchase at prices proportionally exorbitant, whatever necessaries they may require. A lucrative trade of this nature is carried on by the residents of the respective provinces, as well as by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> officers at the outposts with the peasantry under their authority. They procure from the supply of stores which the Dutch company used to send annually from Batavia, such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> as the natives require, particularly blue cloth, which they oblige them to purchase at a price far above its value; and, in order to furnish them with the means of satisfying their wants, the residents lend them <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a> at usurious <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>; so that these people are reduced to the miserable alternative either of submitting to the grossest oppression and fraud, or of remaining destitute of those things which nature and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> unite to render necessary. The accumulated debt in which the peasantry are thus involved, is a never-falling <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONDAGE">bondage</a> and oppression; as it places them entirely at the discretion of their task-masters, to whose bounty they are indebted for their miserable subsistence. An order in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> was published by the Dutch government, some time before the island was conquered by the British, prohibiting the residents from stopping from the peasantry for debts due to themselves, more than two-thirds of the amount of their spice money. But, while the residents retain the extensive powers with which they are necessarily vested, in order to enforce the system of monopoly, the peasantry must be at their mercy; and in that case, the government being tyrannical in its principle, pretexts will never be wanting for evading the force of particular laws. The maxims on which this country is governed are well explained in a Code of written regulations drawn up by order of the Dutch Company some years before the island came into the possession of the British. This Code, in place of containing mild and liberal regulations for the general improvement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>, is filled with all the impolitic restrictions of avarice and despotism; the general tendency of which is, by <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> down and oppressing the lower orders of the community, to strike at the root of national prosperity, and, finally, to impoverish and degrade the country. From a view of those regulations, it appears to have been the settled policy of the government of Amboyna for 150 years back, to discourage cultivation,—to check all attempts to establish <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>,—and, in short, to suppress every improvement which might enable the inhabitants to supply their own wants, and might thus render them independent of the monopolies established by their rulers. In this they have been but too successful; and hence the people are fettered down in a state of the most wretched poverty and dependence,—destitute of the common necessaries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, in consequence of their progressive advance in price; while, in the meantime, the wages of labour have been forcibly depressed, or rather indeed have been kept back from the labourer by fraud; he being bound to the state for a variety of severe duties and services, for which he receives no remuneration. In consequence of these oppressions, the inhabitants are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> and indolent. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> has made no progress. Not more than one-tenth of the island is under cultivation, and it is therefore dependent on <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JAVA">Java</a> for supplies of cattle, and grain. The same causes which have discouraged the cultivation of land and the rearing of cattle, have prevented the improvement of manufactures, or of the mechanic arts; of which the inhabitants are so ignorant, that they do not even manufacture the coarse cloth of which they make their own wearing apparel; but are furnished with it from Java or Ben-

AMBOYNA

Pages 482-483

Amboyna gal, and receive it in retail from the residents and men in office, at such prices as they choose to fix on it. All the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> productions of this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> are in like manner neglected by the policy of its rulers. It formerly produced <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDIGO">indigo</a> of the finest <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. But the growth of this valuable commodity was discouraged by the Dutch, chiefly with a view of protecting the indigo trade carried on between the mother <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> and her colonies in the West Indies; and from a jealousy also, that the natives, by acquiring wealth, might be enabled to assert their independence. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a> grows to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> perfection; but its cultivation is discouraged. Coffee is produced in great plenty in different parts of the island; and, were the culture of it sufficiently attended to, it would be equal in quality to the first Mocha coffee. Wheat might be cultivated to great advantage on the beautiful heights contiguous to the town of Amboyna, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> being well adapted for it. Of maize there is already a great abundance; and the dry and mountain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> is known here; but they have been but little attended to. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit tree grows spontaneously all over the island; but is only made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of by the lowest orders of the people. The cocoa tree also grows here; but the cultivation of it is almost entirely neglected. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the culture of vegetables were sufficiently attended to, this island would produce a great variety of the finest quality. All sorts of roots are produced in abundance, particularly yams and sweet potatoes; and the increased circulation of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, since the island has been in possession of the English, has induced the farmers to bring ample and regular supplies to the market. There is also great variety of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, of the finest quality and flavour. The general appearance of the island is extremely beautiful and picturesque. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">Mountains</a> everywhere covered with lofty woods in perpetual foliage, and valleys clothed in verdure, interspersed with hamlets, and enriched by cultivation, exhibit the most delightful variety that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in those tropical regions is capable of producing. Amboyna was captured by the British in 1796, and restored to the Dutch by the peace of Amiens. It was again taken possession of in 1810, and restored to its former owners by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> concluded in 1814. See Asiatic Annual <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">Register</a> for 1800, p. 200; and Mr Milburn's valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled Oriental <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">Commerce</a>, Vol. II. p. 394. (o.)

UNITED STATES OF. A view of the recent <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of these Republics, of their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STATISTICS">statistics</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> relations, shall be given under the head UNITED STATES.

AMMAN

Pages 499-499

a Physician and Botanist, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a> in 1634. In 1662, he received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">Doctor</a> of Medicine from the University of Leipsic, and, in 1664, was admitted a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> Naturæ Curiosorum, under the name of Dryander. Shortly afterwards, he was chosen Extraordinary Professor of Medicine in the above-mentioned University; and, in 1674, he was promoted to the Botanical <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CHAIR">Chair</a>, which he again, in 1682, exchanged for the Physiological. He died in 1691. Paul Amman seems to have been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of an acute mind, and extensive learning; but a restless and irritable disposition led him to engage too much in controversy, and to indulge in a degree of railing in his writings, which the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the subjects hardly warranted. By his first <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which was published in 1670, under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>, Medicina Critica, seu Centuria Casuum in Facultate Lipsiensi resolutorum variis discursibus acuta, he drew <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon himself the displeasure of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FACULTY">Faculty</a>, who had certainly no cause to rejoice at this exposure of their decisions. In the Paracænemis <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AD">ad</a> discentes circa institutionum medicarum emendationem occupata, which appeared three years afterwards, and in the Irenicum Nuncæ Pompilli cum Hippocrate, which he published in 1689, he showed his independent turn of thinking, by boldly attacking the systems of Galen and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a>, and the abuses to which the implicit <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADOPTION">adoption</a> of them had given rise. But it is chiefly on his botanical writings that his fame ought to rest. The Suppellex Botanica, et Mænuductio ad Materiam Medicam, which he committed to the press in 1675, contains a full, but somewhat prolix, catalogue of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> of the botanic garden of Leipsic and its environs, with their synonyms; followed by a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> introduction to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MATERIA_MEDICA">Materia Medica</a>, which proves an accurate knowledge of the science he was then employed in teaching. His next publication was entitled, Character Plantarum Naturalis, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a> ultimo fine, viz., fructificatione desumptus, et in gratiam philatrorum per canones et exempla digestus; to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> edition of which, in 1685, he prefixed a dissertation on the true classification of plants. In this work he adopted the arrangement of Morison, endeavouring to show, as the title imports, that the genera of plants were only to

ANGLESEY

Pages 634-636

the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONA">Mona</a> of Tacitus, and Tir-mon of the Welsh, is of an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> form; and indented on three of its sides with numerous small bays and creeks; its length from Carnets point to <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANGOR">Bangor</a> ferry is 20 miles, and its greatest breadth from Llanddwyn <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">Abbey</a> to Penmon Priory, 17 miles: its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a>, by the most recent and accurate survey, comprises 173,000 acres. At the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> when <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WALES">Wales</a> was divided into six Counties by Henry VIII. this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-ISLAND">Island</a>, which formed one of them, was subdivided into three <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">Hundreds</a>; at present it contains six Hundreds. In it there are four market <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEAUMARIS">Beaumaris</a> (the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTY">County</a> town), Newborough, Llanerchymedd, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLYHEAD">Holyhead</a>; and 74 parishes. It returns two members to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARLIAMENT">Parliament</a>, viz. one for the County, and one for Beaumaris; is in the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">Province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIOCESE">Diocese</a> of Bangor, and pays one <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a>-tax. The surface is gently undulated; that part which borders on the Menai is finely wooded, but the interior is a naked tract without trees <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> even hedges. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is nearly uniform, consisting of loam of different degrees of tenacity and fertility, with scarcely any clay. It is well watered by 12 rivulets, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> of which are the Braink, Cetini, Ffraw, Llivan, and Allon. Near Aberffraw, where the Ffraw discharges itself into the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, is the lake Llyngoron, about two miles in circumference, abounding in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, gwynaid, and other fish. There is undoubted <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> of the encroachment of the sea on the shore of this Island: the Lavan sands, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of Beaumaris, formed a habitable Hundred in the sixth century, when they were suddenly overwhelmed by the sea. There are five ferries across the Menai Straits, of which Port-hamel, or the Gloomy ferry (so called from the dense woods which in former times overshadowed its banks), is celebrated as the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where Suetonius landed, when he exterminated the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUIDS">Druids</a>. Off the eastern point is the steep, rocky islet of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">Priest</a>-holme, or Puffin's island: it is a noted <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, during the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, of various birds of passage; the Puffin, whence it derives one of its appellations, breeds there in immense numbers. At the northern point of Anglesey, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of Seals; its sides are frequented by vast shoals of fish, and Seals which prey upon them. Anglesey is rich in minerals, particularly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>. Of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">mines</a> of this metal in the Parys mountain, a particular account is given in the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, on the authority of Mr Pennant; since that account was written, the produce of these mines has declined considerably; the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of men employed having been reduced, from 1500 to 600. Besides <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMESTONE">limestone</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, and blue-veined grey marble, sulphat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARYTES">barytes</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> yielding $\frac{1}{2}$ of pure <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAGNESIA">magnesia</a>, steatite, serpentine, fullers earth, and native sulphur, are found in this Island. Hitherto, coal has not been wrought with any profit, though the depth of coal, in proportion to the whole depth sunk, appears favourable, being $3\frac{1}{2}$ feet in 77 feet. An uncommon appearance in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of this fossil is met with in Anglesey, viz. podicles of loose coal of several tons <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. This Island is celebrated for the variety of its shell-fish; Bingley, in his tour, gives a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of thirty-eight of the principal of these productions; the oysters in particular are highly Anglesey esteemed. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">botany</a> of Anglesey presents nothing very peculiar or remarkable. Of the 173,000 acres contained in Anglesey, it is computed that there are 12,600 acres of waste land; and that no more than the eleventh part of the remainder is under tillage, in the following proportions: oats 7953 acres; barley 6107; wheat 520; rye 2. In the *Encyclopedia*, apparently on the authority of the anonymous author of the supplement to Rowland's *Mona Antiqua*, it is stated, that in 1770, upwards of 90,000 bushels of corn were exported, exclusive of wheat. This must be incorrect, as the whole produce of the Island, in the year 1795, taken by an actual survey, did not exceed 59,770 <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>: viz. oats 35,485; barley 22,700; wheat 1578; and rye 7 quarters. The Cattle of Anglesey are of a good breed; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to them; the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a> annual export is about 8000 head, from one to four years old. The Anglesey breed of sheep is the largest in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">North</a> Wales; averaging about 15 lbs. the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, and yielding from $1\frac{1}{2}$ to $2\frac{1}{2}$ lbs. of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>: the annual <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of sheep varies from 5000 to 7000; nearly the same number of hogs are exported. The inhabitants of Anglesey manufacture deep-coloured blue cloth, flannels, blankets, &c. for home <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, but none for exportation. In Newborough there is a manufacture of mats and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, made of the sea reed-grass, which binds together the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> hills on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The antiquities of this Island are sufficiently illustrated in the body of the work. A rural pipe, used by the Shepherd, called the Pibgorn, is said to be almost peculiar to it; it derives its name from its extremities being tipped with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORN">horn</a>; it has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes, besides the aperture in which the reed is concealed; and its tone is between the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> and the clarionet. From the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> returns of 1801, it appears that there were then in Anglesey 6679 houses, inhabited by 7058 families; and 127 uninhabited houses: 9776 persons chiefly employed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">agriculture</a>: 2614 in <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> and trade; and 19,228 not comprised in these two classes: the number of males was 15,775; and of females 18,031. By the returns in 1811, there were 7183 houses, inhabited by 7706 families; 72 houses <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>; 108 uninhabited; 5376 families chiefly employed in agriculture; 1453 in manufactures; and 877 not comprised in these two classes: the number of males was 17,444; and of females 19,601. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be remarked, that, according to both returns, the number of females exceeds that of males; this disproportion is not, however, peculiar to Anglesey, but extends over all Wales. The reader, who is desirous of farther information, in regard to this Island, may consult Davie's *General View of the Agriculture of North Wales*—Bingley's *Tour in North Wales*—Aiken's *Tour in Wales*. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANNEALING">ANNEALING</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and use of this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> in Glass-making, has been already explained in Annealing the body of the work; it remains to add some details in regard to its application to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>. In the manufactures, in which the malleable metals are employed, annealing is used to soften a metal after it has been rendered hard by the hammer, and also to soften <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, which is rendered very hard and brittle by rapid cooling. In the manufacture of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> goods, which are first formed by the hammer, and require to be filed or otherwise treated, and in which softness and flexibility are essential to the change, annealing is absolutely necessary. This is particularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> in making files and scissors; that the metal may be left sufficiently soft for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a>, and for filing off those parts which cannot be ground. Annealing is not less necessary in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of wire, whether iron, copper, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, silver, or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>. The operation of drawing soon gives the wire a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> and elasticity, which, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not removed from time to time by annealing, would prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENSION">extension</a> of the wire, and render it extremely brittle. The same operation is also necessary in rolling or flattening those metals which are in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> state, such as brass, silver, gold, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRAZIER">Brazier</a> who forms vessels of copper and brass by the hammer, can work upon it only for a little time, before he is obliged to anneal it. The common methods employed for annealing iron and steel are very injudicious, and materially injure the latter, when it is used for making cutting instruments. After they have been formed by the hammer, they are generally piled up in an open fire, slowly raised to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and then allowed to gradually cool. By this method, the surface of the steel will be found considerably scaled, from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OXYGEN">oxygen</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>. When it is remembered, that steel consists of iron joined to carbon, it will be evident, that the steel immediately under the scaly oxid will be deprived of its carbon, which has been carried off by the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTRACTION">attraction</a> of the oxygen; and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>, will lose the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, of acquiring that degree of hardness necessary to a cutting <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. Nothing, therefore, can be more obvious, than that steel particularly should be annealed in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> vessels, to prevent that effect. For this purpose, the goods should be placed in a trough or recess made of fire-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or fire-brick, and stratified with ashes, or clean sand, and finally covered with a thick stratum of the same; but if the size of the vessel be small, it may have a cover of its own materials. This oven or trough must now be heated by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FURNACE">furnace</a> passing under and round it till the whole is of a red heat. It must then be suffered to cool, without letting in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The goods so treated, will be much softer than by the common method. The surface, instead of becoming scaled, will have acquired a metallic whiteness, from the presence of a small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of carbonaceous <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> contained in the ashes in which they were imbedded. They will become so <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a> also, as to allow them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> considerably without breaking, which is very far from being the case before the operation. The fracture, before annealing, will be smooth and short; but afterwards it will be rough, exhibiting bright parts of a crystalline appearance. Wire, especially that of iron and steel, should be treated in a similar way, when it is annealed. The wire used for some purposes, requires to be soft, and is sold in that state. If the wire after finishing, when it is bright and clean, were to be annealed in contact with oxygen, it would not only lose all its lustre and smoothness, but much of its tenacity. The process above-mentioned will therefore be particularly necessary in annealing finished wire, as well as in softening it from time to time during the drawing. Copper and brass suffer much less than iron and steel from annealing in the open air, and do not require to be heated above a low red heat. If, however, the lustre is to be preserved, a close vessel would be desirable. The latter metals, after annealing, although much discoloured by the oxygen of the atmosphere, may be cleansed, by immersion in a hot liquor composed of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> and a small quantity of sulphuric or nitric acid. Very small brass or copper wire is frequently annealed, by <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXPOSING">exposing</a> it to the flame of hay or straw. In casting minute pieces of pig-iron, which is generally done in wet sand, the metal possesses the property of steel to such a degree, as to assume, by the rapid cooling, a degree of hardness equal to hardened steel; at the same time, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> are so brittle as to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> by falling on the ground. When, however, these goods are treated in the way above directed, they acquire a degree of softness which renders them penetrable by the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and at the same time capable of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BENDING">bending</a>. In this state, they are much less tenacious than steel, but still so much so, as to have been sold in the form of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTLERY">cutlery</a> for steel. The change which metals undergo by annealing, is not yet thoroughly understood. Most of the malleable metals are susceptible of two distinct forms, one called the crystalline form, which they assume by slow cooling; and the other, the <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a>, which is acquired by hammering or rolling. When this, however, is carried beyond a certain point, the metal becomes so hard, that it is not capable of being bent far without breaking. All the malleable metals in the ingot or in their cast state are brittle, and exhibit a crystalline fracture. By hammering or rolling, they become more tenacious, and break with difficulty, exhibiting what is called a fibrous fracture. At the same time, they become stiffer and more <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>. They lose the latter properties by annealing, but become more malleable. If the annealing, however, be <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a>, the malleability diminishes, and they again have a crystalline fracture. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">Zinc</a> by wire-drawing becomes very flexible, and possesses a degree of tenacity not inferior to that of copper. But, if it be kept in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water for a length of time, it will resume its original brittleness, and show a crystalline appearance when broken. This proves that the particles of metals can change their arrangement, without losing their <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> form—which is still more strongly confirmed by the fact, that brass wire loses its tenacity by exposure to the fumes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, and even by the presence of a damp atmosphere. This is not caused by the moisture, but by the action

ANIMAL ANATOMY

Pages 510-510

I. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">HUMAN</a> ANATOMY. 1. In our supplementary remarks on this first and most important department of Animal Anatomy, we shall endeavour, by the arrangement we intend to follow, to exhibit the outline of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> better adapted, we conceive, for an elementary view of the structure of the Human Body, than that which has usually been observed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of medicine, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> in anatomical works. But it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> be necessary to premise a few observations on the acceptation of certain terms, which will occur very frequently in the descriptions that are to follow. 2. By the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-IMPREGNATION">impregnation</a> or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>, is uniformly meant the moment at which a child, or infant-being, begins to be formed within the womb of the mother. While the child is yet retained within the womb, it is denominated a fetus or embryo; the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> embryo, however, being chiefly applied to it in its earlier stages. The end of the ninth <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> after conception, which is the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> period of birth, is often denominated the full <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The inhabitants of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>, and perhaps of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> in general, are usually full-grown, or adult, at the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of twenty-five or thirty years. This is the [Merged from GENERAL OBSERVATIONS ON THE SKELETON, p.524] I. In the Adult <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">Male</a>. 169. The skeleton of the body may be regarded as the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> frame-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> which supports and contains the softer parts. 170. It is made up of 254 separate pieces of osseous substance, most of which contain a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> called marrow, and are surrounded with a membrane denominated periosteum. These separate pieces, with their appendages, have the appellation of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> usually applied to them; and they are connected to each other in various ways. 1. Of Bones in their separate State. A. Their Osseous Substance. 171. In almost all bones, the osseous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> presents itself under two forms. Externally it assumes the form of an uninterrupted shell or covering, which is called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> part, and a very delicate texture of fine plates or fibres intersecting each other, and leaving small spaces between them, projects internally from this, which is called the cellular or reticulated part. The proportion of these two, varies in different bones. B. Of the Marrow. 172. The chemical properties of the oily matter of the marrow, have not yet been sufficiently investigated. C. The Periosteum. 173. This covering distinctly possesses the structure of tendinous substance. 174. We cannot regard it as correct, that it is prolonged from one bone to another over <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>. In general it covers the whole outer surface of the compact substance, except at those <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> where one bone is united to another. 2. The Connections of Bones. 175. The connections between bones are of two kinds; some admit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, others do not. A. Connections admitting Motion. 176. It may be remarked of those bones which are united in such a manner as to enjoy motion on each other, that their touching surfaces never consist of bare osseous substance, nor even of osseous substance covered with periosteum. They are either provided with separate crusts or prolongations of cartilage, the surfaces of which play directly on each other, constituting what is denominated a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> or articulation; or they are united to one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> intermediate substance, which is <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLEXIBLE">flexible</a>, or admits of compression. a. Articulations or Joints. a. The Cartilages. 177. The surfaces of the portions of cartilage, which are in contact with each other in this <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of connection, are always as smooth as the finest polished <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>. 178. It was affirmed <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago by Dr Nesbit (Human Osteology), and Dr Hunter (Phil. Trans. 1743), and has been much insisted on of late years by Bichat (Anat. Génér.), that these surfaces are covered with a very delicate prolongation of synovial membrane. We are very much inclined to think, however, from a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of experiments, that these anatomists have been mistaken. b. The Ligaments. 179. All articulated bones are partly held together by means of ligaments. These are composed of tendinous substance, and may be divided into fascicular and capsular. The fascicular ligaments are disposed in cords, at intervals, around the joint; the capsular form a continuous web, including the united surfaces in a kind of shut sac. γ. The Synovial Membrane. 180. In all the intervals between fascicular ligaments, portions of synovial membrane may be distinctly seen filling up these intervals. They are attached to the ligaments on the one <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and to the articulated bones on the other, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> at the edge of the cartilaginous surfaces. 181. It does not seem to us, however, to have been yet satisfactorily ascertained, whether this synovial membrane be <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> over the inner surface of the fascicular ligaments; or how it is disposed in joints, of which the ligaments are of the capsular kind. b. Without Articulation. 182. The small bones of the spine called vertebrae, are united to each other chiefly in this way. The portions of them denominated their bodies, are directly connected to pieces of a flexible and compressible substance, somewhat between cartilage and tendon in its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, one piece being common to two vertebrae. B. Connections not admitting Motion. 183. These may be divided into two kinds, suture and synchondrosis. a. Suture. 184. In this <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, the bones are united by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> contact of their osseous substance. The contiguous parts, however, are in general more or less indented or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SERRATED">serrated</a>, the projecting parts of the one being fixed into holes or grooves in the other. The periosteum passes across the line of junction, and does not dip <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> between the united surfaces. b. Synchondrosis. 185. In this mode, a piece of cartilage, or some 3. Dimensions and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">Weight</a> of the Skeleton. 186. The height of the skeleton of a person five feet eight inches, we believe, will be found in general to be about five feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches. 187. Soemmerring (De Corp. Hum. Tab. I.) has made some trials of the weight of the skeleton; and, according to him, it varies from 150 to 200 ounces. But we are uncertain as to the weights he employed, and ignorant of the manner in which his estimates were made. II. In the Adult <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a>. 188. The same general remarks which have just been made with respect to the skeleton of the adult male, apply equally to that of the adult female; only the skeleton of the latter is a little lower, and not so heavy. According to Soemmerring, it weighs in general only from 100 to 150 ounces. III. Before and after Maturity. 189. Parts corresponding to the skeleton may be distinctly perceived in an embryo of seven or eight weeks. At this early period, however, osseous substance has not yet appeared. In the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the future bones, we find either a pellucid substance like jelly, moulded into their general form, and surrounded with periosteum, or else a simple membrane resembling the periosteum in structure. Some bones are wholly gelatinous, others wholly membranous, and others partly in the one state and partly in the other. 190. About the end of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> month after conception, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OSSIFICATION">ossification</a> begins. It does not commence, however, in all parts of the skeleton at once, but takes place at different periods in different bones, or even in different parts of the same bone. Its commencement in some is delayed until a considerable time after birth. 191. When we attend to the progress of ossification in those parts of the fetal skeleton which are at first gelatinous, we observe, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any of these parts are converted into osseous substance so early as the second or third month after conception, they seem to undergo very little previous change of consistence. If they are not ossified, however, till the fourth or fifth month, they gradually lose their resemblance to jelly, becoming firmer, more <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a>, and more opaque; and if the ossification is still further delayed, their opacity, firmness, and elasticity, rapidly increase, they acquire a pearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and are converted into a substance in every respect the same as cartilage. 192. When the ossification commences in this gelatinous or cartilaginous basis, the first part which is ossified is always observed to be situated towards the centre of the jelly or cartilage; and from this point the process gradually extends in every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. In early ossifications, the parts are so minute, that it is difficult to perceive the appearances in the gelatinous basis which immediately precede the formation of the osseous substance. But in those which commence at a later period, the parts of the cartilage which are just about to be converted into bone, uniformly exhibit a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of vascularity; and a number of little <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> specks are observed in them, in each of which a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> blood-vessel seems to terminate, and in which the first <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BONY">bony</a> particles that are formed generally appear. 193. When ossification commences in a membranous part of the fetal skeleton, the osseous substance first appears in the form of a fine <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>-work of slender fibres, confined to a small spot in the middle of the membrane. But by the formation of additional osseous particles, this net-work is converted into a plate of bone of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thinness and delicacy, and having a layer of the membrane covering each surface, which may be regarded as its periosteum. Innumerable bony fibres are then observed to shoot out, in a radiated direction, from the margins of this little plate, and these are soon connected by short transverse threads of osseous substance, in such a manner, as to give the bone for a time a slightly reticular appearance. The spaces between the fibres seem entirely filled up by blood-vessels. 194. In this manner, the ossification extends through the whole membrane, splitting it, as it proceeds, into two layers, which become the periosteum of the opposite surfaces of the new bone, but remain united into one single membrane around the whole of its margin. At the same time, however, that the bone is thus enlarging in breadth, it is also increasing in solidity, from the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEPOSITION">deposition</a> of new osseous particles between those already formed. At last, it assumes the form of a continuous plate of compact substance, the different parts of which are proportioned in their thickness to the corresponding parts of the future bone; and if the adult bone contains any reticulated substance, the cells are generally developed in the middle of this compact plate. 195. No sooner are the cancelli developed in any part of a young bone, than they are lined with a very vascular medullary membrane. This membrane, however, contains only a slightly viscid, reddish, and transparent fluid. It does not appear to begin to receive any admixture of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> till after birth. At first, the proportion of oily matter is small, and it increases in general so gradually, that the fluid does not acquire the consistence or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of true medullary oil, until the period of maturity. 196. In old persons, the medullary membrane seems to become less vascular, and the oil acquires a yellower colour. 197. The periosteum in the fetus is much thicker, and more tender than in the adult. It is more vascular too, and particularly at those parts of a bone where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> ossification is going on. In old persons, it is thinner and less vascular. 198. As soon as the soft <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of the future bones are visible in the fetus, divisions may be observed in them corresponding to the articulations and synchondroses, but none to the sutures. 199. The ligaments and synovial membranes in the young person seem to differ in size only from those of the adult. 200. For a considerable time after the margins of bones, that are intended to be united by suture, first come into contact, they adhere so slightly to each other, that the bones seem chiefly held together by the periosteum which passes from the one to the other. By degrees, however, as the bones are more fully developed, they are locked more firmly into each other. 201. The <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a> of the articulations seems to undergo very little change in the decline of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. But it is not unusual, in very advanced age, to find the cartilages partially converted into osseous substance. On the approach of old age too, we may almost always observe that the sutures begin to be obliterated. Particles of osseous substance are formed between the margins of the bones, the line of the suture is gradually filled up, and at last the bones are fairly continued into each other.

Algebraical View. \[ \frac{1}{r} - \text{ABC}, \&c. = \text{ABC}, \&c. \] is the proposition enunciated in No. 81; \( \frac{1}{r} \) being the value of the perpetuity (112). 193. Examples of the determination of the single premiums for assurances, and of the derivation of the annual premiums from them, have been given in numbers 82—88, also in 95 and 96; but by the algebraical formulae given here, the annual premiums may be determined directly, without first finding the total present values of the assurances. 194. Example 1. Required the annual premium for an assurance on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> \( A \) now 50 years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> 5 per cent. According to No. 185, the operation is thus, \[ \begin{align*} 1 + A &= 12.660 \lambda \\ \frac{1}{1 + A} &= 0.0789890 \times 2.8975663 \\ \text{adding } v &= 0.9523809, \text{ and subtracting unity,} \\ \text{we have } \circ A &= 0.0313699, \text{ agreeably to No. 85.} \end{align*} \] 195. Ex. 2. What should the annual premium be for an assurance on the last survivor of three lives \( A, B, C \), now aged 50, 55, and 60 years respectively, rate of interest 5 per cent? Operation by No. 188. \[ \begin{align*} (68) \quad 1 + \text{ABC} &= 15.001 \lambda \\ \frac{1}{1 + \text{ABC}} &= 0.0666622 \times 2.8238798 \\ v &= 0.9523809 \\ \circ \text{ABC} &= 0.0190431, \text{ agreeably to No. 88.} \end{align*} \] No. 88. 196. Ex. 3. Required the annual premium for an assurance for 10 years only, on a life now 45 years of age, interest 5 per cent. Operation according to No. 186. \[ \begin{align*} v^{10} &= 6.18913 \lambda \times 1.7881068 \\ \frac{1}{v^{10}} &= 4073 \lambda \times 3.6099144 \\ a &= 4727 \times 4.3254144 \\ \frac{1}{v^{10}a} &= 5.28976 \lambda \times 1.7234356 \\ 1 + \frac{1}{v^{10}A} &= 11.347 \lambda \times 1.0548811 \\ \text{Subtract } 6.002 \lambda \times 0.7783167 \\ \text{from } 1 + A &= 13.648 \\ \text{remains } 7.646 \times 1.1165657 \\ 1 - \frac{1}{v^{10}A} &= 4.71024 \times 1.6730430 \\ \cdot 061604 \lambda \times 2.7896087 \\ v &= 0.952381 \\ \circ \text{A} &= 0.019885, \text{ agreeably to No. 96.} \end{align*} \] What has been advanced from numbers 99 to 109, needs no algebraical illustration. (No. 65.) | Ages | Value | |------|-------| | 0 & 10 | 10-649 | | 1 & 11 | 12-275 | | 2 & 12 | 13-087 | | 3 & 13 | 13-769 | | 4 & 14 | 14-106 | | 5 & 15 | 14-334 | | 6 & 16 | 14-419 | | 7 & 17 | 14-432 | | 8 & 18 | 14-395 | | 9 & 19 | 14-321 | | 10 & 20 | 14-221 | | 11 & 21 | 14-106 | | 12 & 22 | 13-987 | | 13 & 23 | 13-864 | | 14 & 24 | 13-797 | | 15 & 25 | 13-608 | | 16 & 26 | 13-483 | | 17 & 27 | 13-359 | | 18 & 28 | 13-255 | ANNULOSA.* The Linnean arrangement of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ANIMAL_KINGDOM">Animal <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KINGDOM">Kingdom</a> has, with some slight emendations, been adopted as the ground-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of the zoological <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> contained in the later editions of the Encyclopaedia. In these Supplemental volumes, we propose to introduce all the recent discoveries in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, and also to avail ourselves of the opportunity thus afforded, of describing the various classes of animals under an arrangement more accordant to the improved views of Science, and to the Order of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>. We shall have occasion fully to explain the principles upon which our system is founded, in the article ZOOLOGY. At present, it is only necessary to mention, that all the different branches of this <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> department of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> will be treated of under these heads: viz. ANNULOSA, CIRRHIPEDAE, INSECTA, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOLLUSCA">MOLLUSCA</a>, RADIATA, and VERTEBROSA. From these heads, references will be made to the zoological articles in the body of the work, and also from the older names to the corresponding appellations in the arrangement adopted in these volumes. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a> ANNULOSA (from Annulus, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> segment), is applied to animals whose bodies are more or less divided transversely into segments. **Class I.—<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CRUSTACEA">CRUSTACEA</a>.** **History.** All the Crustacea, as their name imports, are enveloped in a crust or shell (crusta). Many of the larger <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> were known to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Naturalists. They were named Crustacea by the Latins, Malacostracoi (Μαλακόστρακοι) by the Greeks. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a> has dedicated a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> to the species known to him; Athenæus enumerates those used as food; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> has made mention of such species as were considered useful in medicine. To the observations of Aristotle, very little was added by Pliny; and from his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> until that of Rondeletius, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELON">Belon</a>, Gesner, Aldrovandus, and Johnson, who placed the Crustacea between the Fishes and Mollusca, little or nothing was done that tends in any way to elucidate the natural history or structure of these animals. By the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> reformer Linné, they were arranged under the genera Monoculus, Cancer, and Oniscus, along with apterous insects; but the most prejudiced of his followers now admit that they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> sufficient to establish them as a distinct class. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> of animals was proposed in one of the General Arrangements of the Annales de Muséum, by M. G. Cuvier. It comprehends five classes, the classification of which will form the subject of the present article. As the leading characters of the classes are very obvious, we shall, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, lay them before our readers through the medium of a table, and shall then detail them more fully. - **Class 1. CRUSTACEA.** Branchiae or gills for respiration. Legs † for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. - **Class 2. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MYRIAPODA">MYRIAPODA</a>.** Tracheæ or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-tubes for respiration. Legs more than eight. Head distinct from the thorax. Antennæ two. - **Class 3. ARACHNIDES.** Tracheæ for respiration. Legs eight or six. Head not distinct from the thorax. Antennæ none. - **Class 4. INSECTA.** Tracheæ for respiration. Legs six. Head distinct from the thorax. Antennæ two. - **Class 5. VERMES.** Tracheæ for respiration. Legs none. Antennæ none. J. C. Fabricius, a pupil of Linné, divided the Crustacea from insects, and formed several distinct classes for their reception; but as he has altered his system in his different works, it seems necessary only to state the last, which is given in the Supplement to his Entomologia Systematica. In this work is the following arrangement: - **Class POLYGONATA.** Many maxillæ within the lip. Gen. 1. Oniscus, 2. Ligia, 3. Idotea, 4. Cymothoa, 5. Monoculus. - **Class KLEISTAGNATHA.** Many maxillæ, closing the mouth. Lip none. Gen. 1. Cancer, 2. Calappa, 3. Ocypode, 4. Leucosia, 5. Parthenope, 6. Inachus, 7. Dromia, 8. Dorippe, 9. Orithya, 10. Portunus, 11. Matutin, 12. Hippa, 13. Symethis, 14. Limulus. - **Class EXOCHINATA.** Many maxillæ outside the lip, covered by the palpi. Gen. 1. Albunea, 2. Scyllarus, 3. Pallinurus, 4. Palaeemon, 5. Alpheus, 6. Astacus, 7. Penaeus, 8. Cran-gon, 9. <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol0.html#article-PAGURUS">Pagurus</a>, 10. Galathea, 11. Squilla, 12. Podsydon, 14. Gammarus. Before the publication of this work, Müller (in --- * The animals which compose this type are partly treated of in the Articles ENTOMOLOGY and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">HELMINTHOLOGY</a> of the Encyclopaedia. † For the comparative characters of this type, see Zoology. In the present article, we propose to give the characters and economy of the Genera, and an example of one Species of each, with the exception of INSECTA, which will be treated of under that head in a separate article. ‡ By this term, we <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> those organs which actually perform the functions of legs. A great portion of the species, composing the Entomostraca of Müller, were described by the microscopic observers, Joblot, Frish, Réaumur, De Geer, Baker, Ledermüller, and Geoffroy, and were by the latter author arranged into two genera, which he named Binoculus and Monoculus. By that learned anatomist G. Cuvier, the Crustacea were considered as forming a class, which he placed between the Vermes and Insecta. This indefatigable observer discovered, that the Crustacea breathed by branchiae or gills, and he disposed them into three great sections, viz. I. Monoculus, including the genera, 1. Limulus, 2. Caligus, 3. Cyclops, 4. Apus, 5. Polyphemus of Müller. II. Cancer, comprehending the genera, 6. Cancer, 7. Inachus, 8. Astacus, 9. Palinurus, 10. Squilla, 11. Scyllarus of Fabricius: III. Oniscus, including, 12. Physodes, 13. Omisus, 14. Cymothoa of Fabricius. Lamarck, in his Système des Animaux sans Vertebres, has disposed the Crustacea into the two following orders, viz. Ord. I. ANQUETIL

Pages 735-736

a French historian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, on the 21st of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1723. At the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a> of seventeen, he entered the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> of St Genevieve, where he taught <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and literature with ability and success. He afterwards became <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTOR">Director</a> of the academy at <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHEIMS">Rheims</a>; and, in 1759, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PRIOR">Prior</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a> de la Röe, in Anjou. Soon after this, he was sent, in the capacity of Director, to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SENLIS">Senlis</a>. In 1766, he obtained the Curacy <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Priory of Chateau-Renard, near <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MONTARGIS">Montargis</a>, which he exchanged, at the commencement of the Revolution, for the Curacy of La Villette, in the neighbourhood of Paris. During the reign of terror, he was imprisoned at St Lazare. On the establishment of the National Institute, he was elected a member of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> class, and was soon afterwards employed in the office of the minister for foreign affairs. Endowed with a robust <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which was preserved by a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> equality of temper, and general moderation in diet, Anquetil was capable of very laborious exertions, and is said to have passed ten hours every <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, regularly, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-STUDY">study</a>. When upwards of eighty, he still meditated extensive literary undertakings; but he was carried off by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, in the midst of his projects and researches, on the 6th of September 1808, in the eighty-fourth year of his age. On the evening previous to this event, he is reported to have said to one of his friends, "Come and see a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> who is dying full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>." As an author, M. Anquetil does not stand very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> in the ranks of literature. He possessed more industry in research, than ability or judgment in execution. His style is censurable in many respects, and he appears to have been almost entirely destitute of the critical discernment and philosophical sagacity, which are requisite to form the character of a good historian. The following is a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIST">list</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> works. 1. *Histoire Civile et Politique de la ville de Reims*, 1756-57, 3 vols. 12mo. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is brought no farther <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> than 1657; a fourth volume should have been added, but it never appeared. Anquetil is said to have written this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with one Felix de la Salle, and it is, perhaps, the best of all his productions. 2. *Almanach de Reims*, 1754, in 24mo. 3. *L'Esprit de la Ligue, ou Histoire Politique des Troubles de France, pendant les 16 et 17 siècles*, 1767, 3 vols. 12mo. This work has been frequently reprinted. 4. *Intrigue du Cabinet sous Henri IV. et sous <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIII., terminée par la Fronde*, 1780, 4 vols. 12mo. 5. *Louis XIV. sa Cour et le Regent*, 1789, 4 vols. 12mo; reprinted in 1794, 5 vols. 12mo. 6. *Vie du Marechal Villars, écrit par lui-même, suivie de Journal du la Cour de 1724 à 1734*, Paris, 1787, 4 vols. 12mo; reprinted in 1792. 7. *Precis de l'Histoire Universelle*, 1797, 9 vols. 12mo; reprinted in 1801 and 1807, in 12 vols. 12mo. This work has been translated into English, Spanish, and Italian. 8. *Motifs des Guerres et des Traités de Paix de la France, pendant les regnes de Louis XIV. Louis XV. et Louis XVI.*, 1798, 8vo. 9. *Histoire de France, depuis les Gaules jusqu'à la <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a> de la Monarchie*, 1805 et seqq. 14 vols. 12mo. This work was composed in haste, and is of no <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> value. 10. *Notice sur la vie de M. Anquetil du Perron*. M. Anquetil likewise wrote several papers in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a> of the Institute. See *Biographie Universelle*.

AQUA TOFANA

Pages 754-760

called also <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUA">Aqua</a> della Toffanina, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Aqua della Tofa, from its supposed inventress,—Aqua del petesino,*—Aquetta di Napoli, or simply Aquetta,—a poisonous liquor which was used to a very <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a> and Rome during the latter half of the seventeenth century. Guenin† says, that more people were destroyed by it than by the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a>, which had prevailed a short <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> before it came into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>; and Garelli, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> physician to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">Emperor</a>, wrote to Hoffmann that Tofania confessed she had used it to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> more than six hundred persons. This he learnt from the Emperor himself, to whom the whole criminal <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> instituted against her was transmitted. It is to be regretted, that Garelli, who had such an authentic source of information, has not given us some details of the infamous Tofana or Tofania; as the little that we know of her rests upon the authority of travelers, and is evidently exaggerated, and sometimes irreconcilable with established facts. She was a Sicilian by birth, and resided first at Palermo, and then at Naples. When she began to <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> her horrible profession, is nowhere stated; but it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> presently appear, that it must have been at a very early <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>, and before 1659. She was extremely liberal of her <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, chiefly it is said, to ladies tired of their husbands; and the better to conceal the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of her gift, it was put up in small flat phials, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANNA">Manna</a> of St Nicholas of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BARI">Bari</a>, ornamented on one side with an image of the Saint, that it might <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> for a liquid said to drop from his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a> at Bari, which was in great request on account of the medicinal virtues ascribed to it. Nor is it ascertained how <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> she carried on her murderous practices with impunity and undiscovered. Labat§ says, that when he was at Civita Vecchia in 1709, the Viceroy of Naples, then <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNT">Count</a> Daun, made the discovery. It was long before she was secured, as she was extremely cautious, and often changed her abode or retired into <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">Convents</a>. At last she was betrayed, and, although in a Convent, was seized and carried to the Castel del Uovo, where she was examined. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Pignatelli, then Archbishop of Naples, indignant at the violation of a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> sanctuary, threatened to excommunicate --- * Lanzoni <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a>, 4to. Laus. 1738, Vol. I. p. 69. † Allgemeine Geschichte der mineralischen Gifte, 1st edit. 8vo, Nurnberg. 1777, p. 132. 2d edit. 8vo, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERFURT">Erfurt</a>, 1811, p. 243. ‡ F. Hoffmann Med. <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-RAT">Rat</a>. Syst. P. II. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. ii. § 19. Opera Omnia, 6 vol. folio, Genevac, 1748, Vol. I. p. 198. § Voyage en Espagne et en Italie, 8 tomes 8vo, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, 1730, Vol. IV. p. 33. the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CITY">city</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> she was not delivered up to him, and the people were ready to rise. But the sagacious Viceroy caused a report to be spread, that she and her accomplices had determined upon the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a>, to poison all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> in the city, the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> brought to market, and the public granaries. The manoeuvre succeeded. The credulous people were now clamorous for her <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> with satisfaction the persons whom she accused of having purchased her Aquetta, taken from the Churches and Monasteries. Some of inferior birth were executed publicly; those of higher <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> secretly in prison; and the whole city resounded with the praises of the Viceroy, whose energy had saved it from general destruction. A kind of compromise was entered into with the Cardinal; in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which, after being strangled, her body was thrown at night into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the Convent, by way of testifying some respect for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHTS">rights</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHURCH">Church</a>. But the reverend traveller must have either been misinformed as to the actual execution of this Medea, or she must have been resuscitated; for Garelli expressly says that she was alive in prison at Naples, when he wrote to Hoffmann, not long before 1718; and Keysler, who visited Naples in 1730, likewise asserts, that she was then living in prison, and that few strangers left the city without going to see her. He describes her as a little and very old woman. The Roman ladies very quickly availed themselves of Tofania's discovery; for it was remarked in 1659, that many husbands died when they became disagreeable to their wives; and several of the clergy also gave information, that, for some time past, various persons had confessed themselves guilty of poisoning. This led to the detection of a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> of young married women (who had, for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, an old woman of the name of Hieronyma <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPARTA">Sparta</a>, a pretended fortune-teller), as the perpetrators of these murders. On being put to the torture they all confessed except Sparta, who seemed to rely upon the protection of powerful individuals whom she had formerly served. But she was left to her fate, and was hanged along with her assistant, one Gratiosa. Others were afterwards hanged, or whipt and banished. Sparta, who was a Sicilian, had acquired her knowledge from Tofania at Palermo. Pope Alexander VII., immediately on the discovery and punishment of those who dealt in poison in his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, published an edict forbidding the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISTILLATION">distillation</a> of aquafortis, or the purchase of any of its ingredients, without the permission of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">Government</a>; which Gmelin considers as an artifice to mislead the people as to the real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of the poison, or as originating in the absurd nomenclature of the Chemists of former times, who called arsenic concrete aquafortis. But the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> of the Pope was rendered fruitless; for we are informed by Gayot di Pitaval (Causes Célèbres, Vol. I. Amsterd. 1774, p. 317.), on what authority he does not state, that Tofania's fatal secret was disclosed by the indiscretion of the judges at Naples, to whom she had made confession of her crime. The whole city soon knew that she employed in its composition a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERB">herb</a>, and that its preparation was otherwise easy; and in this way the art of poisoning became very common in Naples, where, Keysler says, it was still secretly practised when he visited <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and Archenholz, who was there in 1780, states, that Aqua Tofana was then in use, although its composition was only known to a few; but <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Frank, who was long Professor in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PAVIA">Pavia</a>, and has written a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on toxicology (Handbuch der Toxicologie, Wien, 1803, p. 168.), regards this as an unfounded calumny, and asserts that it no longer exists or is heard of. Aqua Tofana is described as being as limpid as rock <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and hence it could be administered without exciting suspicion. The Abbé Gagliani adds, that there was not a lady in Naples, who had not some of it lying openly on her toilet among her perfumes, in a phial known only to herself. It was generally believed, that the effect of this poison was certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and that it could be so tempered or managed, as to prove fatal in any determinate time, from a few days to a year or upwards. Four or six drops were reckoned a sufficient dose, and they were said to produce no violent symptoms, no vomiting, or but very seldom, no pains, convulsions, inflammation, or fever; but only a feeling of indisposition, without any very definite symptoms, except sometimes inextinguishable thirst; the victim, however, sunk into a languid state, and his weakness increased daily. Disgust at all kinds of food, and weariness of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, succeeded; the nobler organs were then attacked, the lungs were wasted by suppuration, and death closed the miserable <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a>. This termination was the more certain, that the true cause of these symptoms was not at first suspected, and the remedies <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> prescribed rather aggravated the evil. Indeed, even when known, no treatment was of any avail, although a Dr. Brancaletti, according to Keysler, wrote a book on its remedies, until it was discovered by accident that lemon-juice, when very early administered in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> doses, sometimes proved effectual (Bertholimus), after which, Keysler tells us, that the poison fell into some disrepute. Various accounts of the composition of this detestable liquor have been given. Abbé Gagliani, and more lately Archenholz, state it to be a prepara- --- * Travels through Germany, &c. 4 vols. 4to. 2d edit. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, 1756, Vol. II. p. 368. † J. F. Le Bret, Magazin zum Gebrauche der Staaten-kirchengeschichte, IV. Frank. 1774, p. 131—141, as quoted in the curious <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> on Secret Poisons, in Beckmann's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Inventions and Discoveries—a work which has been of great assistance to us in pointing out authorities. ‡ England und Italien, 5ter Theil Svo, <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol6.html#article-CARLSRUHE">Carlsruhe</a>, 1787, p. 184. || Weckherlin's Chronologen, 12ter Band, p. 146.—L'Espion Dévélisé. Feliciter Audax, London, 1782, p. 61; also Behrends, in Pyl's Magazin für gerichtliche Arzneikunde und medicinische Polizey, B. I. St. 3, 1784, p. 428-477.—Beckmann. § Bertholimus alone enumerates very violent fever as its first effect. See J. J. Wepferi Historia Cicuta Aquatice, 8vo. L. Bat. 1733, p. 372. tion of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CANTHARIDES">cantharides</a> and opium; but this is perfectly inconsistent both with its appearance and effects. By no preparation can the smell and taste of opium, if the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> be sufficient to produce any effect, be concealed, and the acrimony of cantharides is equally connected with its <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>.
