The one of these drugs is highly stimulant, the other a sedative, and neither of them capable of remaining latent in the system, or injuring the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>. Erndtel, * but without any <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, has conjectured that the chief ingredient was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>: <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HALLE">Halle</a> (Die deutenen Giftpflanzen, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a>, 1783) believes, that it was prepared from the frothy saliva gathered round the mouth of a person tortured to death. Garelli, on the contrary, positively asserts it to have been nothing but a solution of crystallized arsenic in a large quantity of water, with the addition, for some unknown reason, of a very innocent herb, the Antirrhinum cymbalaria. The same account is given by Bertholinus, Lobell (Der freymuthige Heilkunstler, Berlin, 1786), Plenk (Toxicologia, p. 335), Haller, + Molitor (Commerc. Lit. Noric. 1737, p. 182), and Möhsen, † and is received by the most judicious systematic writers, as Gmelin and Hahnemann. (Ueber die Arsenikevergiftung, 8vo, Leipzig, 1786, p. 35.) Wildberg, ‡ however, considers its composition to be unknown. From Italy this poison seems to have found its way to Paris. In 1672 Godin de Sainte Croix, an adventurer, who lived in a scandalous intimacy with the Marchioness Brinvilliers, was suddenly killed by suffocation, as it is said, in consequence of the falling off of a mask of glass, which he wore to protect him from the fumes of certain chemical operations about which he was employed. As he had no known relations, his effects were examined by a public officer, and among them was found a casket, containing many packets of poisonous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, sealed up in a mysterious manner, together with a kind of last will, directing the whole to be delivered to the Marchioness, and, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of her having predeceased him, to be burnt unopened. This led to the discovery of his having been instructed in the art of preparing poison, by an Italian, called Exili, with whom he had become acquainted, when confined in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTILLE">Bastille</a>; and of his having furnished the Marchioness with the means of poisoning her father and her two brothers, besides others on whom she tried the effect of her preparations. One of these afterwards was called from her by the name Eau de Brinvilliers. She is also said to have employed a powder called Poudre de Succession. § La Chaussée, who had been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VALET">valet</a> to Sainte Croix, was convicted of being <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCESSORY">accessory</a> to these murders, and was broken alive on the wheel. The Marchioness herself, who had escaped to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LIEGE">Liege</a>, was also seized, and her execution, which took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> on the 17th of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1676, is described with revolting levity by Mad. de Sevigné in a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> to her <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DATE">date</a>. The practice of poisoning, however, did not seem to terminate with the death of this infamous woman; and a particular court called Chambre des Poisons, or Chambre Ardente, was established in 1679, to endeavour to put an end to it. In consequence of the investigations which took place in it, many persons, some of the highest rank, especially the Duc de Luxembourg, were implicated. More than forty persons were at one time confined in the Bastille; but it was ascertained, that almost all of them had been guilty of no crime, but were merely the dupes of a few impostors, who pretended to raise spirits, foretell future events, and to possess many secrets of a similar nature. Two women, La Vigoureux and La Voisin, with the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> of the former, and a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> called Le Sage, ¶ pretended fortune-tellers, were convicted of being dealers in poison, and burnt alive, on the 22d Feb. 1680; some others were hanged, and others acquitted. This closed the proceedings of this inquisitorial court, which has been accused of being a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> engine, contrived to serve the purposes of Louvois and the Marchioness de Montespan. Voltaire, however, admits that the crime of poisoning infected Paris from 1670 to 1680. Concerning the effects of the Eau de Brinvilliers, Pitaval tells us (p. 271,) that the Marchioness's father experienced violent effects from the poison,—extraordinary vomiting, insupportable pain at stomach, and great <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> in the bowels. He died soon after his return from his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>-seat to Paris. The brothers, and five other persons, were all taken ill, and affected with vomiting, after partaking of a tart at dinner. On their return from the country to Paris, the brothers had the appearance of persons who had been long ill; and after suffering, the one for two, and the other for three months, from nausea and vomiting, they died extremely emaciated, and as it were dried up, without fever, though experiencing a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> in the stomach. On opening the bodies, the stomach and duodenum were <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a> and tender, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a> gangrenous and burnt. Mad. Sevigné relates, that the Marchioness often poisoned her husband, that she might marry Sainte Croix, but that the gallant, having no desire for a wife of her disposition, as often gave the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> husband an antidote. She is also said to have attempted to poison her sister; but did not succeed; and that she was in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of trying the effects of her poisons on the --- * Dissert. de Veneno salutem sistens, Lipsiae, 1701, § 21. † Vorlesungen über die gerichtliche Arzneikunde, 2ter Band, p. 190. ‡ Beschreibung einer Berlinischen Medallien-sammlung, 1. Th. p. 148. § Handbuch der gerichtlichen Arzneipraxis, 8vo, Berlin, 1812, p. 224. ¶ Heucher, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MITHRIDATES">Mithridates</a>, sistens preservacionem Principis a veneno, vide ejus Opera, 4to, Lipsiae, 1745, Vol. I. p. 421; also, J. G. Arnold pr. C. G. Stentzell De Venenis terminatis et extemporaneis, quae Galli les Poudres de Succession vocant. This powder was probably an arsenical composition; but it was supposed by Erndtel and Haller to be acetate of lead, and by Brendel (Institutiones Medicinae Legales, Halae, 1768) to consist of lead and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>. ¶ Voltaire, Siècle de <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. chap. 26. poor, and even on the patients in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOTEL">Hotel</a> Dieu, under pretence of charitably supplying them with biscuits. But Voltaire positively denies this horrible imputation, and says, that she never attempted the life of her husband, who overlooked a connection, of which he was the cause. The information concerning the nature of the Eau de Brinvilliers, derived from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of Sainte Croix's famous casket, is not satisfactory. It contained poisons enough to have killed a whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>; besides opium, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LUNAR">lunar</a> caustic, <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a> and vitriol, more than 75 lbs. of corrosive sublimate, and two bottles of a liquid, like water, with a sediment in one. The clear liquid was probably his real poison; as none of the other substances could have been given so as to produce death, without instantly being detected, by their abominable taste; but what this liquid was, we can now only conjecture, for its examination, as reported by Pitaval, shows that the physicians, at that time, had not the slightest notion of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of detecting arsenic even in substance, much less in solution; and accordingly, although both the liquor and powder killed the animals to which they were given, it is candidly admitted, that the poison of Sainte Croix surpassed the art and capacity of the physicians, and that it baffled all their experiments to discover its composition. We have, however, no doubt, that arsenic was the only <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> ingredient of all these pretended secret poisons; as it is the only substance capable of explaining all the credible circumstances related of them. From the mode of administering them in small, but repeated and perhaps increased doses, there was some foundation for the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> that they could be given so as to kill in any determinate time, while their failing in any instance to produce death, was easily accounted for by supposing antidotes to have been administered. But although the progress of knowledge has proved, that there is no such thing as such antidotes, it has on the other <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, by rendering the detection of poison easy and certain, put a stop forever to the trade of poisoners; and what is perhaps of equal importance, to the general alarm and cruel punishment of individuals which have often resulted from <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> deaths being ascribed to poison. It is not because we know less, but because we know a great <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more than our forefathers, that the art of secret poisoning seems to be lost.—See Forensic Medicine in this Supplement. ARACHNIDES. A class of animals of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TYPE">type</a> Annulosa. See <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a> to Annulosa. ARÆOMETER (composed of aquæ, levis, tenuis, and justæ mensura), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of the comparative density and rarity of bodies. The name does not occur in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors; hydroscopium and baryllium being the ancient names of the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>. This instrument was known in the civilized <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Roman empire, about the year 400, as appears from the fifteenth epistle of Synesius, addressed to Hypatia, daughter of Theon; and to Hypatia some <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> writers have erroneously ascribed its <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. The instrument is also described in some verses annexed to Priscian; and the principles on which its operation is founded, are to be seen in the treatise of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHIMEDES">Archimedes</a> on floating bodies (De Humido In- sidentibus). The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TERM">term</a>, as used by writers on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL_PHILOSOPHY">natural <a class="</a>xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, is chiefly applied to instruments which are made to float, so as to indicate the specific gravity of the liquids in which they are placed: the pèse liqueur, and hydrometer, in common use for measuring the specific gravity of vinous spirits, are instruments of this kind. A floating body displaces a portion of the liquid, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of which is equal to its own weight, the liquid acting upwards with a force equal to this weight, and the weight of the body acting downwards with the same force, equilibrium takes place. If the body be afterwards placed in a liquid of less density, the part of the body immersed, will be greater than when the body was in the more dense liquid, because it requires a greater volume of this less dense liquid to equal the weight of the floating body. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> weights of two bodies being the same, their specific gravities are in the inverse ratio of their volumes \( \frac{G}{g} = \frac{v}{V} \), when \( G \) is put for the specific gravity of the first body, \( g \) for that of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a>; \( V \) for the volume of the first, and \( v \) for the volume of the second. On this principle the common hydrometer is constructed; the instrument described by Synesius, is also of this kind. In order that a small <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the volume immersed may be sensible, the part which is intersected by the surface of the fluid is in the form of a very slender <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, the great bulk of the instrument being always immersed in the liquid. At the inferior part is a small <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a>, containing <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> or small lead <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SHOT">shot</a>, which serves as ballast, bringing the centre of gravity low, so that the instrument may float erect, and without much lateral oscillation. The common hydrometers are made of glass, and sometimes of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, or tin or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PEWTER">pewter</a>, and some have been made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> as objects of curiosity: when made of glass, a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>, inscribed upon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, is inserted in the cylindrical stalk; the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of the scale at which the surface of any liquid intersects the stalk, denotes the specific gravity of that liquid. The divisions of the scale should be formed by immersing the instrument in liquids of known specific gravity, and marking a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> corresponding to that specific gravity opposite to each division. The specific gravities of water and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALCOHOL">alcohol</a> mixed in various proportions, have been accurately ascertained by Mr Gilpin (see his Tables, and Dr Blagden's paper in the Philosophical Transactions); on immersing the instrument in a mixture of known proportions of these two liquids, the point at which the surface intersects the stalk, is to be marked with the number expressing the specific gravity of the mixture taken from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a>. Some hydrometers, such as that constructed by the French chemist Beaumé, and which is much used in France under the name of Aréometre de Beaumé, have the Aræmeter scale divided into equal parts, so that the divisions do not correspond as they ought to do with the numbers which express specific gravities. In the aræmeter of Fahrenheit, the uncertainty arising from the erroneous division of the scale is obviated, no division being required. The form of the instrument is the same as that <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> described, only at the top there is a small cup, into which weights are put, so as to bring the surface of the denser liquid to a fixed mark on the stalk; when the instrument is placed in a liquid of less density, some of the weights are taken out till the mark again comes to the surface. Suppose the weight of the instrument and of the weights in the cup together equal to 1000, when sunk to the mark in distilled water at a certain temperature; the instrument is now taken out of the water and immersed in a liquid, where 10 must be taken out of the cup in order to bring the mark to the surface; the immersion in water indicates that a volume of water weighs 1000; the immersion in the second liquid, shows that an equal volume of this liquid weighs 990; when the volumes of bodies are equal, the specific gravities are directly as the absolute weights \( \frac{G}{g} = \frac{W}{w} \); consequently the specific gravity of the second liquid is 990, that of water being 1000. To <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> computation, it is convenient that the whole weight of the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, when in distilled water, at a certain temperature, should be represented by 1000; for this purpose, the instrument-maker divides the weight of the apparatus into 1000 parts, and forms small weights consisting of one, two, three, &c. of these thousandth parts, the relation of which to the ounce or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>, does not require to be known; the weights thus formed are to be used with the instrument. The aræmeter of Nicholson is like that of Fahrenheit, with the addition of an immersed cup, whereby it is rendered proper for ascertaining the specific gravity of solids. Suppose that it requires 400 grains in the exterior cup to sink the instrument to the mark in distilled water, at 60 degrees of Fahrenheit's thermometer: 1st, The body under examination is put into the exterior cup, and weights (say 300 grains) are taken out till the mark again stands at the surface; this gives the absolute weight of the body 300 grains. 2dly, The body is then put into the immersed cup S, taking care to <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> off any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>-bubbles with a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a>, and in order to bring the mark to the surface, a Aræmeter weight (say 100 grains) must be put into the exterior cup, that is, the weight of a volume of water equal to the body, is 100 grains. The first part of the process gave the absolute weight of the body 300 grains, and the volumes being equal, the specific gravities are as the absolute weights, consequently the specific gravity of the body is 300, that of water being 100. This aræmeter may be used to find the specific gravity of liquids; the process, in that case, is the same as that described above in speaking of the aræmeter of Fahrenheit. The aræmeter of Nicholson is useful to the mineralogist for ascertaining the specific gravity of minerals; the specific gravity being a convenient character for distinguishing one kind of mineral from another. It is sometimes made of tinned <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, but where more accuracy is required, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> is the material employed. When put together, it does not exceed a foot in length, and therefore is suited to form a part of the travelling mineralogist's apparatus. Some aræmeters have been constructed with the exterior cup C placed underneath, and supported by a stirrup, whose upper part is fixed to the stalk of the aræmeter, as represented on the margin; this is done in order to place the centre of gravity low, that the aræmeter may thereby float more steadily. The aræmeter floats in a cylindrical vessel fitted to the size of the stirrup, and this vessel is supported on a stand so formed as not to interfere with the free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the stirrup. The aræmeter of Deparcieux is like the common hydrometer, only the ball is much more voluminous; this renders it capable of indicating the small difference which exists in the specific gravity of the water of different springs, for which purpose Deparcieux proposed it. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DILATATION">dilatation</a> of the large glass <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> by heat, has a considerable effect on the operation of this instrument, and this dilatation being different in different instruments, renders the results inaccurate. The different aræmeters above-mentioned, have the advantages of being easily made and easily carried about; but where the specific gravity of a body is required with the greatest accuracy, recourse must be had to the hydrostatic <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">balance</a>, which ought to be constructed with the utmost care by the most skilful <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>. The following algebraic expressions may serve to elucidate some of the properties of the aræmeters hitherto spoken of: \( g \) is the specific gravity of water, which is 1000 ounces when the ounce and foot are taken as units, 1000 ounces avoirdupois being the weight of a cubic foot of water. \( z \) is the diameter of the wire-stalk of the aræmeter. \( \pi \) is 3.1415, &c., the number expressing the periphery of a circle whose diameter is 1. When the small weight, the density of the liquid, and the length of that part of the stalk which is submerged on adding the small weight, are known, then this equation will give the diameter of the stalk in known quantities \( z = \frac{2}{\sqrt{\frac{w}{v + \frac{1}{3}x^2}}} \). When the weight of the whole araeometer is known in ounces, &c., and the specific gravity of one of two liquids (water for instance) is known, the difference of specific gravity between that liquid and another liquid may be had in known quantities. \( g \) is the specific gravity of water. \( g' \) is the specific gravity of the second liquid, which is here supposed more dense. \( w \) is the weight of the volume of water displaced by the araeometer. \( s \) is a small additional weight placed on the exterior cup to keep the araeometer, when placed in the denser liquid, at the same point of immersion as when it floated in water. \( w + s \) is the whole weight of the apparatus when floating in the denser liquid. The equation \( g' = \frac{w + s}{v + \frac{1}{3}x^2} \) is obtained by substituting \( g' \) for \( g \), and \( w + s \) for \( w \) in the equation, \( g = \frac{w}{v + \frac{1}{3}x^2} \), which was given above. Divide by \( g = \frac{w}{v + \frac{1}{3}x^2} \) and there results \( \frac{g'}{g} = \frac{w + s}{w} \), which gives the proportion of the density of the second liquid to the density of water. By <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SUBTRACTION">subtraction</a> there results \( \frac{g' - g}{g} = \frac{s}{w} \) and \( g' - g = \frac{s}{w} \), that is, the difference between the density of the second liquid, and the density of water is found by multiplying the small weight by 1000 ounces, and dividing this product by the number of ounces, &c., which denote the weight of the araeometer unchanged. Small bodies, whose specific gravities are known, serve to indicate the specific gravity of a liquid in Aræometer, which they just remain suspended. In this way, beads of glass, three or four tenths of an inch in diameter, are employed, each of which remains suspended in spirit of a certain specific gravity. The density of each of these beads, or rather bubbles, is regulated by the proportion between the quantity of glass and the cavity which the glass incloses. A piece of bees-wax, whose specific gravity, by the addition of lead, is such, that the body is just suspended in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRINE">brine</a> of a known density, is used as an araeometer in some <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> works. The fresh <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a> of a common fowl is just sustained by brine of a certain specific gravity, and is employed as an araeometer. The araeometer of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a>, consists of a phial, Homberg's, with a slender neck and glass-stopper, so made, that it may be filled with the same volume of different liquids. It is employed in finding the specific gravity of liquids in the following way: 1st, The phial is filled with distilled water, and then weighed in a balance; 2dly, The phial is emptied, and again filled with the liquid, whose specific gravity is sought, and weighed in a balance, the proportion of the weight of the contents of the phial in the second process to the weight of its contents in the first, is the specific gra- The pressure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> supports columns of different <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a>, whose height is inversely as the densities of the fluids. An arrometer has been constructed on this principle. It is a curved tube, one leg of which has its extremity immersed in water, and the other in the spirit whose density is to be tried. On rarifying the air in the tube, by means of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PUMP">pump</a> fixed at the upper part of the tube, the water ascends in one leg, and the spirit in the other; the height of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of each liquid being measured by a scale of equal parts applied to each branch of the tube. This instrument has never come into use, probably on account of the difficulty of ascertaining, with precision, the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> at which the surfaces of the columns are terminated. See Encyclopaedia, Art. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HYDRODYNAMICS">HYDRODYNAMICS</a>, Part I. ch. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. 2. for some farther notice of Arrometers.

ARABLE LAND

Pages 337-338

We shall endeavour to arrange all the most important details connected with this first <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> of our subject under the eight following sections: 1. Of implements and machinery: 2. Of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARM">farm</a>-buildings: 3. Of fences: 4. Of tillage: 5. Of following: 6. Of the cultivation of the different crops: 7. Of the order, of their succession: 8. Of the various substances used as manure, and the modes of applying them.* * We have not thought it necessary to make Soils the subject of a separate <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECTION">section</a> under this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a>, because the article in the body of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> contains nearly all that can be said in regard to them, in a popular way. Those who wish to go further may consult the Elements of Agricultural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, by Sir Humphry Davy, whose observations we could not have abridged with any advantage in this <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">Sect</a>. I. Implements and Machinery. The numerous implements of tillage husbandry may be arranged under these six heads—such as are employed, 1. In preparing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAND">land</a> for semination; 2. In depositing the seed; 3. During the growth of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; 4. In reaping and securing the crop; 5. In preparing it for market; and, 6. In the general purposes of a farm. But as the same implement is sometimes used for more than one purpose, it would be of little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> to adhere strictly to this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any other arrangement. The implements required for rendering land fit for tillage do not belong to this <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> of the article, and several others that have not yet been brought into general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, or are employed only for particular purposes, shall be noticed under the sections to which they respectively belong. 1. Ploughs. Of ploughs there are a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many different sorts; and, besides the variety of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> occasioned by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of soils, and the different purposes for which they are employed even on the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, there is a considerable diversity in the form, in districts where both the soil and the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of culture are nearly alike. The most obvious general distinction among ploughs is, their being constructed with or without <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a>; and each of these kinds may be again distinguished by other circumstances—such as the form of the mould-board and share; their operation in making one or more furrows at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; their size; and the depth at which they are calculated to work, as in trench-ploughing. It would neither be of much utility, nor at all consistent with our limits, to describe all the numerous varieties of form. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the operation to be performed, and the rules for constructing ploughs that shall be adapted to the different purposes of the cultivator, have been already pointed out in the body of the work; and, therefore, all that is necessary here is to mention those ploughs that are in most general use, in the best cultivated districts. The Swing-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">Plough</a>, with a feathered sock or share, and a curved mould-board, is almost the only one used in Scotland, and throughout a considerable part of England. The old Scotch plough mentioned in our former article has been laid aside, except in a few of the least improved counties, where it is still found useful, when the soil is encumbered by roots or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. The swing-plough is drawn with less power than wheel ploughs, the friction not being so great; and it probably admits of greater variations in regard to the breadth and depth of the furrow slice. It is usually drawn by two horses abreast in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> tillage; but for ploughing between the rows of the drill culture, a smaller one, drawn by one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> employed. A plough of this kind, having a mould-board on each side, is also used both in forming narrow ridges for turnips and potatoes, and in laying up the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> to the roots of the plants, after the intervals have been cleaned and pulverized by the horse and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> hoe. This plough is sometimes made in such a manner, that the mould-board may be shifted from one side to the other when working on hilly grounds; by which means the furrows are all laid in the same <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>—a mode of construction as old as the days of Fitzherbert, who wrote before the middle of the sixteenth century. This is called a turn-west plough. Swing-ploughs, similar to the present, have been <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> known in England. In Blythe's Improver Improved, (Edit. 1652,) we have engravings of several ploughs; and what he calls the "plain plough" does not seem to differ much in its <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> parts from the one now in use. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AMOS">Amos</a>, in an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ESSAY">Essay</a> on Agricultural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACHINES">Machines</a>, says that a person named Lunnus (whom he is mistaken in calling a Scotchman, see Maxwell's Practical Husbandman, p. 191.) first attempted its construction upon mathematical principles which he learned in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>; but having obtained a patent for the making and vending of this plough, he withheld the knowledge of these principles from the public. However, one Pashley, plough-wright to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Turner of Kirkleatham, having a knowledge of those principles, constructed upon them a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of ploughs. Afterwards his son established a manufactory for the making of them at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTHERHAM">Rotherham</a>. Hence they obtained the name of the Rotherham plough; but in Scotland they were called the Dutch or patent plough."—"At length the Americans, having obtained a knowledge of those principles, either from <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> or Holland, claimed the priority of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>; in consequence of which, Mr Jefferson, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> of the United States, presented the principles for the construction of a mould-board, first to the Institute of France, and next to the Board of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> in England, as a wonderful discovery in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>." (Communications to the Board of Agriculture, Vol. VI. p. 487.) According to another writer, the Rotherham plough was first constructed in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a> in 1720, about ten years before Lunnus's improvements. (Survey of the West Riding of Yorkshire.) But the present improved swing-plough was little known in Scotland till about the year 1764, when Small's method of constructing it began to excite <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>.* This ingenious mechanic formed the mould-board upon distinct and intelligible principles, and afterwards made it of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>. His appendage of a chain has been since laid aside. It has been disputed, whether he took the Rotherham or the old Scotch plough for the basis of his improvements. The swing plough has been since varied a little, in some parts of Scotland, from Small's form, for the purpose of adapting it more completely to particular situations and circumstances. Of late this plough has been made entirely of iron. See Plate I. Wheel-Ploughs, used in many parts of England, Wheel-are also constructed in a great variety of forms. Their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> recommendation is, that they require less skill in the ploughman; but it is admitted, that the friction caused by the wheels adds to the resistance, and that they are more expensive, and more liable to * Small's Treatise on Ploughs and Wheel <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARRIAGES">Carriages</a>, 1784; and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Kames's <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">Farmer</a>.

ARAUCANIA

Pages 760-765

a territory on the western <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of South <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>, extending 186 miles in length, between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> Biobio and <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-VALDIVIA">Valdivia</a>, and penetrating 420 miles inland to the foot of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDES">Andes</a>. The lower parts of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are included within its limits, and the whole superficies which is bounded by 36° 44' of south latitude on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, and 39° 50' on the south, occupies about 78,120 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> miles. Originally, Araucania was of smaller dimensions, not reaching above 300 miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-shore; but it received a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GREAT">great</a> accession by the union of another territory belonging to the tribe Puelches, in the course of the seventeenth century. This is a pleasant and fertile <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, partly consisting of wide and extensive plains, partly mountainous, with spacious valleys interposed. It contains two considerable <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, Laquen, called Villarica by the Spaniards, 72 miles in circuit, with a conical islet in the centre; and Nahuelguapi, 80 miles in circuit, which also has an islet towards one side covered with trees. The latter is the source of a river of the same name, which, after a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LONG">long</a> course, falls into the ocean, near the Straits of Magellan; and the Talton, which discharges itself farther north into the sea, rises from the latter. A great volcanic mountain, fourteen miles in circumference at the base, and visible at the distance of 150, stands near the lake Villarica. Its eruptions are not violent, though it is always in an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> state. The summit is covered with snow, but lower <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, perpetual verdure is intermixed with woods, and besides mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, several streams flow from it. Sulphur and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">Salt</a> are plentiful on Araucania, the eastern confines; and quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMBER">Amber</a>-grease are thrown up on the coast. <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINES">Mines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a>, formerly yielding immense revenues, are said to exist in the southern parts, but ever since the natives expelled their Spanish invaders, they have prohibited resorting to them under pain of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. Possibly all <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol9.html#article-REMEMBRANCE">remembrance</a> of their site is lost, and the Araucanians are sufficiently prudent to avoid awakening the cupidity of neighbouring nations by discovering it. This precious metal is not rare beyond their confines. We are acquainted with the vegetable productions of this territory, only in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with those of the surrounding country; they are numerous, useful, and afford a copious supply for the sustenance of mankind. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and utility of a tree called the Pehuen, probably a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>-fruit, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of some analogous <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, is particularly celebrated, as uniting the properties of the Pine, Chestnut and Frankincense. It is of spontaneous growth, requiring no culture, and rises 80 feet in height, by about 8 in circumference; the whole tree at full size being of a pyramidal <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> are conical, and its fruit, which is as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> head, is divided into cells, containing kernels resembling chestnuts. These are ate in the same way, or sometimes reduced to flour, and preserved by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>. A yellowish odoriferous <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GUM">gum</a> exudes through the bark. The sea abounds in fishes, and various phœne frequent the shores. Of these the sea Elephant is the largest, often being 22 feet in length, and 15 around the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; it produces more <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> than the rest; and is so fat, that undulations under the skin are perceptible during its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. Furious combats ensue among the males for possession of the females, which latter always retire until their issue; and that for the most <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> is in the death of one or other of them. Their skins are generally covered with scars; yet notwithstanding the great size of the animal, and its warfare among its own species, a smart blow near the nose is invariably fatal. A species of Hippopotamus is said to inhabit some of the lakes and rivers of Araucania, different from that of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, but its existence is not sufficiently authenticated. However, it is only of late years that Naturalists have become acquainted with the real Hippopotamus, whose figure and habits were long considered to be fabulous. One of the most useful animals in this country is the Chililhueque, a species of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIMINUTIVE">diminutive</a> camel, greatly resembling the sheep, about 4 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, of various colours, grey, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> very soft <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, which is employed solely in manufacturing the finest cloths. Formerly, it was used as a beast of burden; now it is highly prized by the inhabitants, by whom it is never killed except at festivals, or on occasion of solemn sacrifices. The natives of the country now described, are called Inhabitants Araucans or Araucanians from the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Arauco, which forms a small portion of it. They denominate themselves <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARA">Ara</a>, which signifies free, or unsubdued, though some European authors have affirmed, that both Auca and Araucanian originated with the Spaniards, as a name of reproach, signifying rebel or <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAVAGE">savage</a> banditti; and others, such as Falkner, says, that they denominate themselves generally moluches or warriors. Whatever may be the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, they are a The Araucanians do not differ from the ordinary stature of mankind; their persons are handsome; they are of a strong muscular form and martial appearance; their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> is of a reddish brown, clearer than that of the other Americans; they have round faces, small expressive eyes, and small flat feet. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEFORMITY">Deformity</a> among them is very rare. The women are of a fine delicate figure, and many, especially of one of their tribes called Boromees, are beautiful. The Araucanians possess uncommon vigour of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, which is probably augmented by their free and uncontrolled <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. Inhabiting a delightful country, and unaccustomed to that variability of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> which generates lasting distempers, they rarely become grey before attaining sixty or seventy years of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGE">age</a>; many are to be seen who have reached an hundred; and to the latest <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, their personal and mental faculties remain equally entire. These people are said to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> high in moral character; they are intrepid and patient of labour, enthusiastic admirers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, which has gained them the name of invincible from their enemies; courteous, and hospitable. But these good qualities are sullied, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not altogether obscured, by numerous vices. They are prone to all kinds of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a> and debauchery: they are haughty and presumptuous, entertaining a profound contempt for other nations, and considering <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> the only genuine source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>; sentiments which powerfully conspire to keep barbarians barbarous. Not content with exercising their prowess against their neighbours, they practise invasions of each others <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, and carry off quantities of spoil. But notwithstanding their <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> violence, these private dissensions are generally confined to pilage, without bloodshed, for deadly weapons are seldom resorted to. Their animosity towards the Spaniards being originally roused by <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUST">just</a> provocation, has remained for centuries unabated; and, in their incursions into their settlements, they have sometimes put all the men to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, while the women were spared, and carried into <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CAPTIVITY">captivity</a>. They have been called faithless and treacherous by that <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>; but most probably more from resisting oppression, than from truly meriting such reproaches. The Araucanians being a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> people, have adopted a suitable costume, consisting in clothes fitted <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the body, and a mantle or cloth, called poncho, with an opening in the middle, to admit the head. Some of these are of so fine and elegant a texture, as to sell for an hundred, or an hundred and fifty dollars. The head is begirt by a wreath of embroidered wool, and ornamented with beautiful plumes, during warfare. <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MODESTY">Modesty</a> and simplicity equally distinguish the dress of the women, which is entirely of woollen stuff, and consists of a piece descending to the feet, a girdle, and a cloak, called ichella; the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> floats gracefully in tresses over their shoulders, and their heads are decorated with a kind of false <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMERALD">emerald</a>, that is held in great estimation. Necklaces and bracelets are also wore for ornament, and rings on every finger. The national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> for all the apparel of both sexes, especially among the lower classes, is greenish blue. The Araucanians never inhabit <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>: their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of independence has deterred them from living in places surrounded by walls, which they consider a mark of servitude: hence they dwell in cottages or hamlets scattered on the banks of rivers, or on plains: and, as their local attachments are strong, each family prefers occupying the same bounds which have served for the subsistence of its forefathers. The houses are simple, kept remarkably clean and neat, and proportioned to the size of the family. They are surrounded by trees, under which they partake of their meals, in the open <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> during <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>; and the wealthy are then fond of displaying their plate. These people are much less carnivorous than most uncivilized tribes, neither do they esteem fish grateful food, and they live chiefly on what is prepared from different kinds of grain. At their feasts, however, or marriages, funerals, and such public occasions, remarkable profusion prevails: three hundred individuals are then sometimes present; the feast lasts two or three days, and as much provision is consumed as would maintain an ordinary family during two years. Fermented liquors form a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> ingredient of the entertainment, and the guests testify great dissatisfaction, should they be at all sparingly supplied with it, whatever may be the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of property being anxious to entertain his friends, Bacchanalian revels succeed each other, almost without interruption; and they are the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> occupation of the Araucanians, when free of warfare. Celibacy is thought reproachful here. Both sexes <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>, in that state are exposed to contemptuous expressions, and polygamy is practised to an unbounded <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>. A man marries as many wives as he can afford to purchase, for the father of each <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> receives a price on her being transferred to a husband. Marriage is attended with apparent violence. The husband, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> with the father of his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRIDE">bride</a>, accompanied by some friends, lies in wait near a certain <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, where she knows she is to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>. Notwithstanding her shrieks, and affected resistance, she is placed behind him on horseback, and is conducted with much clamour to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, where her relations receive the covenanted presents, after having partaken of a feast. The expense on such occasions is so considerable, that none except the rich can afford to marry many wives; and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POOR">poor</a> are generally content with one or two. The first, however, is alone respected as the real or legitimate spouse; all the others are held in a secondary view; and she has the whole arrangement and regulation of the internal <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> concerns. But it is no easy <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> for the husband to repress the jealousy and rivalry excited by the jarring inclinations of his different wives. Each must daily present him with a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DISH">dish</a> of some food prepared by herself, in her own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> or fireplace; for which reason, the Araucanians have a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fires in their houses equal to that of the women inhabiting them, and the most polite way of inquiring of any one how many wives he has, is asking "how many fires he keeps?" Each wife must, besides, supply her husband with a poncho or cloak yearly. They entertain great respect for their husbands; and in addition to their domestic duties, Araucanians, they have to perform all the most laborious operations. Both sexes practise several daily ablutions, in the course of which they become expert swimmers and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a>, and they are able to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> the largest rivers with great facility. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-READING">Reading</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> are no part of the accomplishments of the Araucanians, nor can they be induced to acquire either; but they hold oratory in high estimation. Children are accustomed from an early period to speak in public, and are carried by their parents to the national assemblies, where the best Orators of the country display their eloquence; therefore much <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to speaking correctly, and preserving their <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> pure. So great is their precaution to avoid the introduction of any foreign expressions, that if a stranger <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in their territory, he is compelled to abandon his own name, and assume one in the Araucanian language. The Missionaries who preach in the national language with the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of making converts, are frequently interrupted by the audience when an <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ERROR">error</a> escapes them. The speeches of the Araucanian Orators are said to be highly figurative, allegorical, and elevated; they contain all the essential parts of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>, and are constructed by its rules. Their style is impressive, and seems capable of being directed to the passions. They are fond of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, which is expressed in blank <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VERSE">verse</a>, not in <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RHYME">rhyme</a>, and, like that of all barbarous nations, is employed on warlike exploits. Its images are bold, lively, and animated; for it has been truly observed, that unrestrained enthusiasm is the chief characteristic of the poetry of the uncivilized. Their learning, however, is very limited, and certainly the cultivation of poetry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> not readily <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to its improvement. In physic, the Araucanians <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in simples, or the practice of ceremonies; and their leading <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> ascribes the origin of all diseases to insects or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WITCHCRAFT">witchcraft</a>. Ordinary remedies are resorted to for destroying the former; but for the latter, a different course is followed. The physician having lighted up the patient's room, desires the women to sing a doleful tune, to the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-ACCOMPANIMENT">accompaniment</a> of drums, while he fumigates the patient; and a sheep, about to be sacrificed, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. Having killed the animal, and sucked some blood from its heart, he approaches the patient, pretending to inspect his belly for <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POISON">poison</a> which has been administered by some sorcerer, and then falls into a pretended swoon, accompanied by frightful contortions. While the sick person's relations question him concerning the cause of the evil, he answers in a manner the most suitable to the occasion, or fixes an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> on some individual, which frequently leads to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> of the innocent in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> of the supposed injury. Their physicians, however, are capable of reducing dislocated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a>, and setting fractured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>; they can even perform wonderful cures of wounds, and have a slight skill in dissection. The Araucanians divide the year into twelve months, the names of which are characterized by their properties, as Avuin-cuyen, the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>; Cogi-cuyen, the month of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>; Huin-cuyen, the unpleasant month; Hacul-cuyen, the first month of winds; thus somewhat resembling the Prairial, Floreal, Nivose, in the revolutionary language of the French. They divide the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DAY">day</a> into twelve parts, each Araucanian equal to two hours with us in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>. The stars are classed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSTELLATIONS">constellations</a>; they are acquainted with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>; and some among them even entertain speculations of their being other inhabited worlds. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMETS">Comets</a> are supposed to originate in terrestrial exhalations united in the higher regions; and they call eclipses the death of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOON">moon</a>. Few generations can avail themselves of the knowledge of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a>, or preserve their own to posterity, where writing is not practised. They have little acquaintance with the arts, and are ignorant of the principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>; chiefly employed in warfare, they are accustomed to constant privations, and thence abstain from those luxuries which are the offspring of a state of peace and the arts. Their principal manufacture consists of ponchos or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> cloaks, which some years ago they were wont to dispose of to the extent of 4000 annually, either to the neighbouring tribes or to the Spaniards: their other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of traffic are cattle, horses, feathers, and baskets of curious workmanship. They have the character of strict integrity in commercial transactions, which are conducted entirely by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BARTER">barter</a>. They have no <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and for their own commodities receive wine, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and hardware. The <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the Araucanians bears some <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> to the feudal system, but it does not appear, that, as in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, their lands are held by military <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>. The whole territory is divided into four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> districts called Uthal-mapus, being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARITIME">maritime</a> country, the plains, the country at the foot of the Andes, and that which is occupied by part of these mountains. Each district is subdivided into five provinces, and each province contains <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> counties; therefore their total possessions are partitioned into an hundred and eighty parts. Each Uthal-mapu is governed by a chief, styled Toqui or commander, subordinate to whom are the Apo-Ulmenes, and on these, in so far as respects military affairs, are dependent, the Ulmenes, under whose immediate jurisdiction the counties are placed. All these orders have badges of distinction; the Toqui a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HATCHET">hatchet</a>, the Apo-Ulmen a silver-headed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATON">baton</a>, encircled by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> on the middle, the Ulmen a baton simply with a silver head, and their dignities are <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>. The whole combine in a great national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> usually held in a plain, where the pleasures of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TABLE">table</a> usually divide their attention with state affairs. This <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> council is vested with the power of declaring war; and the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTION">election</a> of a military commander in chief, immediately follows a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> to that effect. Should none of the Toguis be themselves qualified for so important a station, any other person whatever may be chosen, even one of low rank: and on his appointment he assumes the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Toqui, bears the stone hatchet, which is laid aside by the rest, who now take an oath of fealty to him. He regulates the number of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> to be furnished by each portion of the state, and nominates the higher officers, who have the choice of their own subalterns. Meantime ex-warfare presses are secretly dispatched to all the allies of the nation, announcing the approach of hostilities: which are intimated by investing the envoy with a bundle of Araucanía. Arrows tied together with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> string; but if they have actually commenced, the finger of a slain enemy is added to the arrows. The armies consist of five or six thousand men, cavalry and infantry, though some authors who have written on this subject, deny that the whole country can produce such a force: the infantry is divided into regiments, of 1000 each, containing ten companies of 100 men: the cavalry is divided in the same manner, but the numbers are not always alike: their arms are swords and lances; those of the infantry, pikes or clubs pointed with iron. The onset of these troops is terrible; they bear every thing before them, and always try to cope <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> to hand with their foes. Each soldier, as was the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of Europe in feudal times, carries his own provisions, which consist only of a small bag of parched <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEAL">meal</a>; and this diluted with a little <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, generally proves sufficient subsistence until reaching an enemy's country, where he can live at free <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Their conflicts are conducted with great desperation, though, at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, wonderful regularity and subordination are preserved; but as all pant after military glory, and as valour is the only path to fame, the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> is eagerly courted, where rank after rank is successively destroyed before defeat or victory can be declared. The <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> over, and the spoils of war divided by equal portions, according to numbers, not in proportion to rank, the next <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> is a horrible sacrifice of one of the unfortunate captives to the manes of those who have fallen, called Prolancon, or the dance of the dead. Many barbarous nations, nay some emerging from the darkness of their savage state, have been accustomed to offer up human sacrifices; and all mankind have believed, at one period or other in their progress to civilization, that blood was grateful to their Deities, or that it was necessary for the repose of their deceased relatives. Some, less cruel and sanguinary, have been content with the destruction of the lower animals; but others, more atrocious, have shed the blood of their own species. This deliberate murder has been of three distinct descriptions: first, to propitiate Divinities, or to avert their wrath; secondly, that the victims might be useful to deceased persons passing to a future state; and thirdly, that the manes of those who had fallen in war might be appeased. The Prolancon, nevertheless, is seldom resorted to; but, when determined on, it is conducted with great formality. The miserable prisoner is seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>, deprived of its ears and tail, with his <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FACE">face</a> turned towards his own country, and ignominiously conducted amidst a circle of the Araucanians and their chiefs. There he is obliged to dig a hole in the ground, wherein a number of rods are <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> in succession; and while he repeats the names of the warriors of his nation, the surrounding soldiers accompany his words with contempt and execrations. He is next ordered to cover the hole, as if to <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol1.html#article-BURY">bury</a> the reputation and value of his fellow warriors, whom he has just named. Then the Togui, or one of his bravest companions, ambitious of the honour, dashes out the brains of the unfortunate victim with a club. But the solemnity is not yet completed; for, with cannibal-like ferocity, his heart is instantly torn out, and presented to the Chief, who, sucking a little of the blood, transmits it to his officers, to follow his Araucanía example. Should the skull of the prisoner not have been fractured by the violence of the blow, a cup is made of it, which, as is told of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Scythians, is used at the succeeding banquets. Meanwhile the soldiers strip the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> from off the bones, in order to procure them for flutes; and, having cut off the head, carry it on a pike around their circle, stamping a measured <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>, and vociferating the war song of Savages. In the next place, the head of a sheep is applied to the mangled corpse, and the whole ceremony closes with a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of riot and intoxication. Should a truce follow victory or defeat, and both, or either side be weary of the contest, the parties meet in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CONGRESS">congress</a>, and an Araucanian Orator makes a speech on the evils of war, the advantages of peace, and the most eligible means of mutually preserving it. A branch of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>-tree is here a pacific <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a>, as that of the olive is elsewhere. If the enemies are Spaniards, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">President</a> or leader makes an answer adapted to the circumstances of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>; and articles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> having been agreed upon, several chiliqueques are sacrificed for its permanence. The Chiefs of each party then participate of a meal together, and presents are distributed to those of the Araucanians. It is affirmed, that, as the latter suffer least from warfare, and conduct it without much difficulty, they never sue for peace, and thence that the first overtures always proceed from the Spaniards, with whom they have incessantly been engaged in bloody and destructive contests. But it is rather to be inferred, from the best authorities, that they have not invariably felt equal confidence; and that their numbers, at the end of a war, have been so greatly diminished, as to make them as desirous as their foes of pacification. A congress must frequently be repeated, as without it, the Araucanians, a haughty <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, would consider themselves neglected and despised, and go to war for no other reason. The civil code of these people is very limited, and, as well as their criminal laws, rest entirely on consuetudinary principles, none being written. The latter chiefly respect the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> of murder, robbery, witchcraft, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADULTERY">adultery</a>, and treachery, which are all <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> offences. The murderer, however, can escape by a pecuniary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> with the relatives of the deceased; and husbands and fathers are not subject to any punishment for putting their wives or children to death, because they are judged to be the natural masters of their lives. Persons accused of sorcery are first tortured by fire, on purpose to obtain a discovery of their accomplices, and then stabbed with daggers. Execution immediately follows the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> is sometimes administered in a very <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> and tumultuous manner. Impatient of delay, the Araucanians often <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LAW">law</a> of retaliation in lesser offences, which leads to the subversion of all public order, and is the source of many enormities in their turn becoming the objects of this kind of retributive justice. The <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of the Araucanians is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of absurdity invented by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DESIGNING">designing</a> or superstitious, and imposed on the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BLIND">blind</a> and credulous whom they found ready to receive it; but, amidst that absurdity, containing some principles which have generally Araucania, been admitted by the more reflecting part of mankind. They are said to believe in a Supreme Being, who has subordinate Deities, like their own subaltern officers. One of these is the god of war, another a benevolent, and a third a malevolent <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, who is called Guecubu. This last is the most active <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGENT">agent</a> of all others, and the source of every misfortune. If a horse dies, it is because the Guecubu has rode him; if the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> trembles, it is because the Guecubu has given it a shock; nor does a person ever die, who is not suffocated by the Guecubu. Such is the language of the Missionaries, from whom alone our principal knowledge of the Araucanians is derived. However, these Divinities receive no <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADORATION">adoration</a>; they have no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a>, and only on occasion of some severe calamity, or the conclusion of a peace, are sacrifices offered to them. Then the Araucanians immolate animals, and burn tobacco, which is esteemed the most grateful incense. The Supreme Being, and the benevolent Deity, are invoked on urgent occasions,—those which most naturally induce mankind to seek the protection of superior powers. Christianity has never made any progress among this nation; and although the Missionaries are well treated, respected, and allowed ample liberty to preach their doctrines, they are utterly unsuccessful in making converts. The Araucanians are extremely superstitious; they have implicit confidence in omens and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>, particularly such as may be gathered from <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DREAMS">dreams</a>, or the flight of birds; and he who has confronted death with intrepidness in battle, will tremble at the sight of an owl. They entertain uncommon apprehensions of pretended sorcerers, who they imagine keep under control a kind of beings partaking of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of men and animals, concealed in caverns by day, but let loose to transform themselves into nocturnal birds, that shoot invisible arrows at their enemies as they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRAVERSE">traverse</a> the air. On all occasions they consult Soothsayers, who boast of their own powers, and give firm <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a> to their predictions. The <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOUL">soul</a> is a principle admitted by the Araucanians; they maintain that the human frame is compounded of two substances essentially different, one destructible on death, the other incorruptible and incorporeal, which exists for ever. They have also wavering <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> about a place of future reward and punishment, situated to the west beyond the sea; but regarding the actual state of the virtuous or the vicious, they are not agreed. Their funerals are ceremoniously conducted. The body of the deceased, clothed in his best attire, is laid on a high bier or scaffold, where it remains during the night, and the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> is passed by the relatives in weeping, or in eating with those who come to offer consolation. This meeting is called caricahuin, or the black entertainment. On approaching the place of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERMENT">interment</a>, a woman walks behind strewing ashes on the way, to prevent the soul, it is supposed, from returning to its late abode; and the body being laid on the ground, is surrounded with arms and other instruments, and covered with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PYRAMID">pyramid</a> of earth or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Sometimes a horse is killed and inclosed among them. But no sooner do the relatives retire, than, according to their ideas, an old woman comes in the shape of a whale, to transport the deceased to the Elysian fields, though before his arrival, a toll is exacted by another Araucanian old woman guarding a very narrow passage, who malevolently deprives the passenger of an eye, in event of refusal. In this <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-ELYSIUM">Elysium</a> the same functions are exercised by the souls of the deceased as on earth; husbands have the same wives, but the latter have no children, because that region cannot be inhabited by any but the spirits of the departed. They may revisit their own country, still possessing the same properties as when united to the body; and the Araucanians conceive that the tempests of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">thunder</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> which they witness, originate from their furious combats in the air. A storm never happens among the Andes, or on the ocean, which they do not ascribe to a battle between the souls of their deceased countrymen, and those of the Spaniards; the roaring of the wind is the trampling of their horses; thunder the rolling of drums; and lightning the flashes of their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>. If the course of the storm travels towards the Spanish frontier, they believe that the spirits of their countrymen are victorious; if it approaches their own territory, they are overwhelmed with consternation, and encourage them to be firm and resist their enemies. Though the Araucanians wander about their own country, they are rarely seen out of it, unless while waging war; sometimes they cross to the eastern parts of South America, and, meeting with another tribe called Pampas, repair to Buenos-Ayres, there passing for the people of that nation. Our knowledge of their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> is limited nearly to the period when the American Continent was visited by Europeans in the fifteenth century; and as they are themselves destitute of written records, it must be sought among the Spanish Chronologers. About the year 1450, an Inca of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PERU">Peru</a> attempted the conquest of the extensive region of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHILI">Chili</a>, and consequently, of Araucania along with it; but his <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> retired on being defeated in a sanguinary engagement. A century later the Spaniards having gained a firm establishment in America, resolved to extend their conquests, but were obstinately opposed by the Araucanians with a body of 4000 men, led beyond their own confines; and their conduct on this occasion, though they did not prove victorious, impressed their enemies with apprehensions which have never abated. The Spaniards were at length enabled to form settlements within their boundaries; and sometime after, Pedro de Valdivia, a celebrated officer, was defeated in a pitched battle, taken prisoner, and dispatched with the blow of a club, about the close of the year 1553. A period of bloody warfare followed, which cost the Araucanians the life of their favourite commander Lautaro, whose talents were held in the highest esteem. Though sufficiently exasperated before, their resentment was inflamed still farther against the Spaniards for their barbarous mutilation of those unfortunate prisoners who fell into their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>.
