Figs. 1 and 2, are two elevations of a Bone-mill, the first being taken in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, to show the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> wheel and the length of the rollers, and fig. 2, at the end, to show the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> passing through the rollers.—The water wheel, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AA">AA</a>, is represented as being of the overshot kind; it is included between the two walls, BB, upon the top of which, the pivots <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> gudgeons of its axis are supported in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> bearings. A <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> formed on the end of one of the gudgeons, is received into a square socket, at the end of the connecting axis, D, which communicates the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to the lowest, F, of the two rollers, the latter having a similar square on the end of its axis, to be received into the socket at the end of the connecting axis, D. The rollers are supported by a wooden frame, GG. Two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> frames, HH, are bolted <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon it, having grooves, or openings in them, of nearly the whole length, to receive the brasses for the pivots of the rollers, as shown in fig. 2. At the upper ends of these grooves, are screws, h h, by which the rollers can be made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> at a greater or less distance from each other, as the size of the bones which are to <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through them require. Two pinions, k l, are placed upon the ends of the axles of the two rollers, and by their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> acting together, they compel the two rollers to accompany each other. The surfaces of the rollers are filled with indentations and strong teeth, which penetrate and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the bones to pieces. This is accomplished, by employing separate <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-CAST">cast</a> iron <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WHEELS">wheels</a> placed side by side upon an axis, to compose the rollers; the wheels have coarse teeth similar to those of a <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a>, or ratchet wheel; each wheel of the lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>, F, is an inch thick; and they are placed at distances of an inch and a half asunder, having circles of hard wood or iron, placed between them, which are two inches less in diameter. Thus they leave grooves, between the toothed wheels, which have the effect of rendering the teeth upon the surface of the roller insulated. The wheels of the opposite roller, E, are 1½ inch wide, and the spaces between them only 1 inch; and the two are so situated, with respect to each other, that the teeth upon one, are opposite to the spaces between the teeth of the other, as is clearly explained by the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>. A hopper, II, is fixed above the machine, over the rollers, and into this the bones are filled, so that they rest upon the two rollers, and are drawn in by their motion, the teeth penetrating and breaking every piece however <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> it may be. The bones should be supplied rather gradually to the machine at first, to avoid choking it, and the rollers should then be adjusted to a considerable distance asunder; but when the bones have once passed through in this way, the rollers are screwed closer by the screws, h h, and the fragments ground a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WILL">will</a> generally be found sufficient, as it is not advisable to reduce the bones to a state of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DIVISION">division</a>. The pinions must have deep cogs, to enable them to take deep hold of each other, when the rollers are set at only half an inch distance to grind fine, and without the cogs being liable to slip when the centres are separated, so far as to leave a space of 1 inch, or 1½ inches, between the rollers, for the passage of the large bones the first time. The rollers will act most effectually, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the different wheels are fixed upon their axles in such a position, that the teeth will not correspond, or form <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to the axes, and then no piece of bone can escape without being broken by some of the teeth. The bones which have passed through the rollers, slide down the inclined board, R, and collect at the bottom in a large heap. When all the stock of bones are thus coarsely broken, a labourer takes them up in a shovel and throws them again to the hopper, to be ground a second time. Fig. 3. A machine for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> Potatoe Flour. Machine for A, a <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a> covered with tin-plates, pierced with holes, so as to leave a rough surface, in the same manner as the graters used for nutmegs, &c., but the holes in this are larger. This cylinder is situate beneath a hopper B, into which the potatoes are thrown, and thence admitted into a kind of trough C, where they are forced against the cylinder, which, as it revolves, grinds the potatoes to a pulp. Motion is given to the machine by a handle fixed upon the end of the axis of the grating cylinder A, and on the opposite extremity of this axis is a fly-wheel D, to regulate and equalize the movement. The potatoes, when put into the hopper, press by their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> upon the top of the cylinder, and, as it revolves, they are in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-PART">part</a> grated away. On one side of the lower part of the hopper is an opening, closed or opened, more or less, at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol10.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, by a slider d, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of opening which this has regulates the passage of the potatoes from the hopper into the trough C. This is as wide as the length of the cylinder, and has a concave board R fitted into it, which slides backwards and forwards by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of levers a, fixed to an axis extended across the frame of the machine, and a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-LEVER">lever</a> N is fixed upon this axis, and carries a weight which acts upon the board R, by means of the levers, to force or press forwards the potatoes contained in the trough C against the cylinder, and complete the grating of them into a pulp. The tin-plate covering the cylinder is of course pierced from the inside outwards, and the bur or rough edge, left round each hole, forms an excellent rasping surface. Fig. 4. A Potatoe-scop. A, The end of the handle, having a round stem, which passes through a piece scop. of metal D, and has then a semicircular <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTER">cutter</a> E fixed to it. This is sharp on both edges, and turns upon a pivot, shewn by the dotted lines, fitted in a similar piece of brass to D, which, as well as the latter, is formed out of a piece of plate BC. This forms a shield to hold the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> firm upon the potatoe, by placing the thumb of the left <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HAND">hand</a> upon the shield BC, and pressing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of D into the root, which is grasped in the hand; then, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the handle half round with the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand, the semicircular knife makes a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-SWEEP">sweep</a>, and cuts out a piece or set, which is a segment of a small sphere. Fig. 5. is an end view of the shield BC, and the knife E, also the piece of brass D, placed upon the surface of a potatoe F, in which the dotted line FG shews the piece the knife will cut out by its motion.
